title: Building Zonelyte: from an AI prototype to a tool my team could use
excerpt: What building a timezone workspace taught me about AI prototyping, Firebase, early feedback, and the work between a demo and a product.

source.title: I Built a Timezone Tool for Distributed Teams Using Google AI Studio (The Free Lovable Nobody’s Talking About)
source.editorialNote: Edited from my original build story. Pricing comparisons and the inconsistent model-release timeline have been removed; product details describe the original March 2026 account.

children.text: My team works across three continents. Scheduling a call often meant opening several timezone tools, passing screenshots around, and asking people to check the calculation again. We could see what time it was in each city. Deciding when to meet still took a conversation.
That was the problem behind Zonelyte: a shared view of a team's working hours, with enough context to choose a meeting time together. The useful unit was the team, not the clock.
Start with a decision someone already makes

I had been sitting on the idea for months. It was the kind of small project that could easily remain a private repository forever. What changed was getting to a visual prototype quickly enough to use it while the problem was still fresh.

I described a timezone grid to Google AI Studio: multiple cities, working hours shown through colour, and a way to highlight overlapping slots. In the original build, the first version took about 45 minutes. It used React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, and it looked coherent enough that I kept opening it.

That last detail mattered more than the speed. A prototype can be technically impressive and still tell you very little about whether anyone needs it. This one helped me perform a task I already had. It gave me a reason to return.
Keep the shared data model small

I had been using Supabase as my default for new projects. For Zonelyte, I tried Firebase. The core operation was simple: load a workspace, read its locations, and show changes to everyone looking at it.
The original workspace model reflected that simplicity:

body.code:
workspaces/{shortId}
  locations: [...]
  name: string
  createdAt: timestamp

children.text: Firestore's real-time updates fitted that interaction. I did not need a complex reporting model to answer the first product question. I needed a small shared document and a responsive view of it.

This was a choice for this workload, not a general verdict on databases. A product centred on relational queries might lead me somewhere else. The lesson was to choose around the operation the product performs most often, rather than reuse a default without questioning it.
Add accounts where they create value
The first version had no authentication. A workspace could be shared through its URL without asking the team to create accounts. That made it easy to put the tool in front of colleagues.

Saved personal presets introduced a different need. A person's favourite cities should follow them between devices and be available from the browser extension. That was a reason to add sign-in, without turning it into a requirement for the basic shared view.

AI Studio generated the initial Google sign-in integration. I still had to handle the surrounding details: script-loading order, the credential exchange with Firebase, and popup behaviour. These were small pieces of the interface, but they determined whether the experience actually worked.
Generating the outline was fast. Debugging those boundaries was where I learned the system. I would not describe the generated version as finished simply because the happy path looked convincing.
Put it in front of colleagues early

When I shared a link with the team, people added their cities and responded with concrete requests. Could they drag across a range of times? Could they share the workspace without making everyone register? Could the colours be easier to distinguish in dark mode?
Those requests were more useful than a speculative roadmap. They came from someone trying to make an actual meeting happen.

The feedback shaped proposal slots, reinforced the no-account sharing flow, and led to another pass on the palette. It also exposed a mistake in my process: I had waited weeks to share something that could have produced useful feedback much earlier.
Change tools when the work changes

As the codebase grew, I moved more of the work into Claude Code. The task was no longer simply to sketch a grid. It involved understanding existing components, changing several files together, and reasoning about state across the application.

AI Studio helped me explore the interface and reach a useful first version. Working inside the repository gave me a better place to handle refactoring, real-time synchronisation, the extension, and shared-workspace URLs.
I found the combination more useful than expecting one workflow to cover every stage. The question was what context the next change required, and which environment made that context available.
A prototype is the beginning of the work

By the time I wrote the original post, the product included shared workspaces, meeting proposals, calendar export, a Chrome extension, and a dark theme. The stack was React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, and Firebase.

The first convincing prototype took less than an hour. Turning it into a product took months of evening work. Both statements are important. AI shortened the distance to something tangible; it did not remove the need to understand the system or observe people using it.

If I started again, I would show the first usable version to colleagues sooner, keep the initial data model small, and choose each AI workflow around the stage of work. I would also be more precise about what “built” means. A generated screen, a working demo, and a tool someone depends on are different milestones.

title: AI progress, and the developers living through it
excerpt: A revised personal reflection on AI-assisted development, career uncertainty, engineering judgment, and the distance between capability and dependable work.

source.title: AI, AI, AI, AI and it was good YearAI
source.editorialNote: Revised from my January 2026 essay. Unsupported numerical claims, attributed quotations without sources, and broad predictions have been removed. Personal observations remain identified as personal observations.

children.text: At the start of 2026, I did not want to write another list of model releases. I wanted to talk about what it felt like to work in software while the tools, expectations, and career conversations were changing around us.

From Portugal, my experience of the job market did not resemble the optimism of every AI announcement. I saw competition for roles, pressure on salaries, and developers wondering how to position themselves. That was my observation, not a comprehensive labour-market study. It was still worth discussing.
The question behind my original essay remains useful: when the technology becomes more capable, what improves for the people using it?
Capability and a sustainable career are different questions

An assistant that can produce a useful first implementation changes the work. It can help someone explore an unfamiliar library, understand a repository, or turn an idea into a prototype. I have felt that change directly in my own projects.

It does not follow that every developer becomes more productive by the same amount. A person who can recognise a good solution, diagnose an error, and define a useful test has a different relationship with generated code from someone who has to accept it on trust.

That distinction worries me when I think about people entering the profession. If a team delegates its simpler tasks to an assistant, it still needs a way for junior engineers to learn how the system works. Removing the task without replacing the learning opportunity creates a problem that better code generation will not automatically solve.
Judgment becomes easier to see

When a first draft is cheap, decisions around it become more visible. Is this the right problem? What must remain true after the change? What evidence would convince us that it works? What should the system do when a dependency fails?
These questions were always engineering questions. AI makes them harder to avoid. A convincing implementation can arrive before the team has agreed on the behaviour it actually needs.

I do not think the answer is to abandon programming knowledge. Understanding code is part of judging it. The practical shift is to connect that knowledge to requirements, architecture, review, and operations rather than treat typing speed as the main measure of contribution.
Generation does not settle verification
A code change can look tidy, pass a narrow test, and still misunderstand the product. It can also preserve the intended behaviour while introducing a permission mistake or an operational surprise.

My concern is the gap between how quickly we can propose a change and how confidently we can accept it. Filling that gap takes explicit expectations, tests that exercise meaningful behaviour, and reviewers who understand the consequences of the change.

The answer is not a blanket rule that every AI-generated line is suspect. Human-written changes need the same discipline. The difference is that a high volume of plausible output makes weak review habits more expensive.
Competing globally does not require becoming generic

Remote work widened the set of people we can work with. AI tools also make some skills easier to access. That can feel threatening if a professional identity rests entirely on producing a familiar kind of implementation.

The response I find useful is specificity. Understand a domain. Learn where its systems fail. Become good at explaining tradeoffs and delivering a result someone can rely on. Show the decisions behind the work, not only a list of frameworks.

This is an approach to developing a career, not a guarantee of employment. Geography, timing, company budgets, and personal circumstances still matter. Treating uncertainty as an individual failure would miss much of the problem.
Keep space for disagreement

Using several assistants does not remove the need for independent thought. Agreement can be useful evidence, but it is not proof. If several outputs follow the same assumption, their consistency may hide the very question a reviewer should ask.

For architecture work, I want the alternative made explicit. What would make this choice wrong? What constraint would favour a different design? What evidence are we missing? Those questions turn a polished answer into something that can be examined.
Build a future we want to work in

I think about these changes as an engineer and as a parent. Seeing several technological shifts within one lifetime is exciting. Constant adaptation can also be exhausting. Both reactions can be true.

I do not have a final answer for what AI will mean for every career. I do have a direction for my own work: use the tools, understand their boundaries, keep learning, and make the reasoning behind important decisions available to other people.

The measure of progress should include more than what a model can generate. It should include whether a team can trust the result, whether newcomers can learn, and whether the people doing the work have a sustainable place in it.
That is the question I wanted to ask in January. It still seems more useful than another leaderboard.

title: From a school charity market to a New Year’s Ideas Generator
excerpt: A paper box of celebration ideas became a small bilingual web app. A project note about preserving the human interaction that made the idea work.

source.title: New Year’s Ideas Generator launch
source.editorialNote: Expanded from my original launch post. The stack and features describe the December 2024 release.

children.text: At my children's school charity market, we had a small paper box filled with ideas for celebrating New Year. People picked an idea, received a sweet, and reacted to the surprise. It was a simple interaction, but it made people smile.

I wanted to make a digital version of that experience. During evening coding sessions, I built a New Year's Ideas Generator: a small web app that offered a suggestion without asking people to plan the entire celebration first.
Preserve the interaction that worked
The paper version did not need instructions. Pick something from the box and see what you get. That clarity was the part worth carrying into the application.

It would have been easy to turn the idea into a large planning tool. But a planning tool asks for decisions before it gives you anything. The original interaction did the opposite: it offered a starting point, and the person could decide what to do with it.
The app's purpose was to make that first step easy. The surprise mattered, and so did the ability to try again.
Add useful constraints without losing the playfulness
Not every celebration idea suits every situation. Someone with a small budget or a quiet evening ahead should not have to keep rejecting elaborate suggestions.

The release included filters for budgets and energy levels. It also supported English and Russian, reflecting the languages in our family. Sharing made it possible to pass an idea to someone else rather than leave it on one screen.

These were modest features, but each helped preserve the original experience in a different setting. The filters made suggestions more relevant. The language choice made the interaction accessible to more of the people I had in mind. Sharing carried some of the social element of the market into the app.
Let the presentation serve the moment

I added animations and confetti because the interaction was about a celebration. A little movement made sense here. It was part of the response to receiving an idea, rather than a separate demonstration of what the interface could do.

The application used Next.js 14, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. I published it as a free, open-source project and made it usable across devices. Those are details of the original release, not a claim that this is the stack every small project should choose.
A small project can have a clear reason to exist
My children were the first testers and the inspiration for the idea. The project started with something I had watched people enjoy, rather than a search for a feature list to implement.

That is what I want to remember about it. Useful side projects do not always start with a large market or an elaborate plan. Sometimes they start with a small interaction that deserves to travel a little further.
The challenge is to notice what made it work, then avoid burying that quality under the implementation.

title: Specifications that outlast the model
excerpt: Models change quickly. A clear description of intended behaviour gives an engineering team something stable to build and review against.

source.title: Chapter 10: what survives when models and tools turn over
source.editorialNote: Expanded from my short note on Chapter 10 of From Copilot to Colleague. The practical example below is an illustrative addition, not a reported project result.

children.text: Chapter 10 of From Copilot to Colleague asks what survives when models and tools turn over. In my original note, I pointed to an idea from Al Harris and the Kiro team at AWS: use specifications to describe what a system should do, rather than prescribing every implementation detail.
The attraction is practical. A model can change. A framework can change. The behaviour people rely on should remain something the team can describe and check.
Make the intended behaviour inspectable

A request such as “improve the booking flow” leaves most of the important decisions unstated. It does not explain what is wrong, what success looks like, or which existing behaviours must be preserved.

A specification can make those decisions available to the implementer and the reviewer. It should explain the trigger, the expected result, and the conditions under which the result must hold. It should also say which questions are still open.
This does not require a large document. It requires enough precision that two people can discuss the same behaviour rather than imagine different versions of it.
An example: changing a meeting time
Consider a scheduling tool. “Handle timezones correctly” is a reasonable intention, but a poor acceptance criterion. An implementer needs to know what the user is changing and what should stay fixed.

An illustrative requirement could be: when a participant changes their display timezone, the meeting keeps the same instant, while its displayed local time changes. Changing the timezone must not silently reschedule the meeting.

That statement gives the team a behaviour to test. It leaves room to choose the date library and state-management approach. It also makes a review more concrete: did the implementation preserve the instant, or did it change the event?
Keep the specification close to the evidence

A specification is useful only while it describes the intended product. When a decision changes, the document and its checks should change with it. Otherwise, an assistant can follow the document accurately and still produce the wrong behaviour.
I find it helpful to think of the specification as part of the working system: a place where intent can be reviewed, disagreements can be resolved, and tests can be connected to a reason.
The goal is not to write enough prose to eliminate judgment. It is to give judgment something concrete to work with.
Why this belongs at the end of the book
A book about AI engineering can become dated if all its value rests on the names of current tools. I want readers to leave with ways to reason about the work after those names change.

Describing a desired outcome clearly is one of those habits. So is checking whether the delivered result matches it. Together, they make it easier to adopt a new assistant without handing it an undefined problem and hoping its interpretation is the right one.

title: What local AI meant to my work at the end of 2024
excerpt: A revised year-end note on government-contract projects, local language models, and choosing a useful workflow before choosing a model.

source.title: 2024 AI year-end reflection
source.editorialNote: Expanded from my December 2024 reflection. Absolute claims that local models automatically make data safe or reduce costs have been replaced with conditional tradeoffs.

children.text: At the end of 2024, the AI work I was most excited about involved helping teams find opportunities in government contracting. It gave the technology a concrete purpose: support a difficult business task, rather than add a chat interface simply because one was possible.

I was also working with Shamim Bhuiyan on Generative AI with Local LLM. The book and the project work connected around a practical question: how can we make AI useful while staying deliberate about where data goes and how the system operates?
Start with the work, not the model

Government-contract information is a good reminder that having access to text is not the same as making a useful decision. A team needs to understand whether an opportunity fits, what the requirements mean, and what deserves attention.
A model may help with parts of that process. The quality of the overall workflow still depends on what information it receives, how its output is checked, and where a person makes the final decision.
That is the perspective I wanted to carry into 2025: begin with a recurring problem and a useful output. Only then decide which model or agent workflow belongs in the solution.
Local execution is a design choice

In the original social post, I described local models as a way to protect data and reduce costs. That was too absolute. Local execution changes the available tradeoffs; it does not settle them automatically.

Running inference locally can reduce reliance on an external inference provider. It also gives the team responsibility for the machine, the application, its access controls, and the other services connected to it. A local model does not make a networked application isolated by default.

The cost question is similarly conditional. Hardware, utilisation, maintenance, and the quality needed for the task all matter. A comparison is useful when it covers the actual workflow, rather than only the price of one model call.
Learn by building a small complete workflow

The direction of the book was hands-on: give developers a way to work with local models and understand the surrounding application. A small complete example can teach more than an impressive but disconnected demonstration.
The useful questions are concrete. What data does the application need? What result does it return? Where can it be wrong? How will someone notice? What happens when it cannot complete the task?
These questions give experimentation a purpose. They also make it easier to compare approaches, because the desired outcome stays stable while the implementation changes.
Keep the optimism, make the claims narrower

I ended 2024 enthusiastic about AI and the open-source work around it. I still want to preserve that enthusiasm in this archive. The revision is to be more careful about the promises attached to a deployment choice.
Local language models are worth understanding because they create options. Whether those options improve a particular product depends on the constraints and the evidence from using it.

title: Returning to coauthoring: from Apache Ignite to generative AI
excerpt: Seven years after our Apache Ignite book, Shamim Bhuiyan and I returned to writing together with a hands-on guide to building AI applications.

source.title: Getting Started with Generative AI announcement
source.editorialNote: Edited from my original book announcement. The launch used the title Getting Started with Generative AI; the book is now presented on this site as Generative AI with Local LLM.

children.text: In September 2024, I shared a milestone: Shamim Bhuiyan and I were writing together again, seven years after our book on Apache Ignite. I had missed the collaboration.

The new project was a hands-on guide to building AI applications. In the original announcement, I called it Getting Started with Generative AI. Readers of this website will find it under Generative AI with Local LLM.
A different subject, a familiar collaboration

Apache Ignite and local language models belong to different parts of the technical landscape. What connected the projects for me was the opportunity to turn engineering work into something another developer could learn from.

Writing together also meant sharing the work of explaining it. A technical idea can make sense in conversation and still need considerable care before it works on the page. Collaboration gives that explanation another reader while it is still being formed.

My original post was mostly an announcement and a thank-you. That remains the right centre of this note. The milestone was not simply adding another title to a list; it was returning to a working relationship I valued.
A practical route into the subject

The book focuses on building with local language models, with material intended for developers who want to connect the concepts to applications. The accompanying website provides the current description and ways to find the book.
I would rather point readers to that maintained information than preserve an old social-media announcement as if it were a current specification of every chapter or tool version.
The original post also thanked colleagues who were sharing their own work on AI. That sense of exchange was part of the appeal: learning, building, and making the results available to other people.
Thank you to Shamim for the collaboration, and to the readers who have followed the work from distributed computing into AI.

children.text: In November 2025, I shared that the Russian edition of our generative AI book had arrived from Bombora Publishers. My coauthor, Shamim Bhuiyan, was signing copies in Moscow. I was in Portugal, waiting for my own copy and following the delivery tracking.
After spending so much time with a book as a working document, there is something satisfying about knowing that physical copies are making their way to readers.
A milestone beyond the manuscript
The original announcement mentioned the book reaching Chitay-Gorod stores in Moscow. That was a snapshot of the launch, not a promise about where the book can be bought today.

The part that mattered most to me was more personal. I hoped that one day I could visit a bookstore with my daughters and show them the work. A project that lives on a screen can be difficult to explain. A book on a shelf gives it a different kind of presence.
I was also looking forward to signing copies for friends after my delivery arrived. These are small details beside the technical content, but they are part of what makes publishing memorable.
Credit belongs to the collaboration
This was another moment to thank Shamim. The work reached this point through a shared effort, and I want the archive to keep that credit visible.

title: Missing Directus translations? Check the related collection permissions
excerpt: A debugging note from my Stack Overflow answer: separate the translation query from the permissions needed to read the related records.

source.title: Fetch items from Directus Api — my answer
source.editorialNote: Expanded from my August 2025 answer, with an illustrative request and a link to current query documentation. Adapt collection and field names to your own schema; the example has not been executed against your Directus instance.

children.text: I answered a Directus question in August 2025 after running into a problem retrieving translated article content. It looked like a query problem. The important discovery was that reading an article did not automatically establish access to the related translation records.

The lesson from that debugging session was simple: check the relationship and the permissions independently. A more elaborate request will not compensate for a related collection the requesting identity cannot read.
Isolate the smallest useful request

Before combining nested fields and language filters, try to retrieve the translation record directly using the same identity as the failing request. In the example I was working with, the relevant collection was articles_translations.

That gives you a smaller question to answer. Does the record exist? Is it linked to the expected article? Does its language value match the one being requested? Can this identity read the collection and the requested fields?
If the direct request fails, there is little value in adding more complexity to the parent article query. Resolve the narrower problem first.
Make the nested request explicit

Once the underlying access works, ask for the fields you need and apply the language filter to the translations relationship. The following request illustrates that shape. Its collection and field names are examples, not a universal Directus schema.

Here, the top-level filter selects an article, while the deep filter constrains the returned translations. The locale must match the value stored by your application. Do not assume that ar and ar-SA are interchangeable identifiers in the data.
Directus documents field selection, filters, and nested query parameters in its
query parameter guide
. Check that guide alongside your actual schema when adapting the request.
Fix the permission that is missing

In my original answer, querying the translation collection directly helped expose what was wrong. The lasting lesson is not to grant broad access until the response appears. It is to establish exactly which read permission is required by the operation.

Keep the identity consistent during the comparison. A successful administrator request does not explain why a request made by the application fails. Test the operation in the context that is actually producing the error.
Keep the diagnosis separate from the final query
There are two useful artefacts at the end of this exercise: a small request that demonstrates access to the translation, and the application request that returns the desired article content.

Keeping both makes the reasoning easier to revisit. If the behaviour changes later, you can determine whether the failure is in access, the relationship, or the shape of the request without starting the investigation from scratch.

title: Installing your first local LLM: a small, useful starting point
excerpt: Start with one local model, verify inference, and understand the boundary between your machine, its network, and optional tools.

source.title: Installing your first local LLM: a small, useful starting point
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies. The old version-specific claim about network binding has been removed.

children.text: A useful first local AI project is simply getting a model to answer a question on your own machine. That gives you a foundation for later work with retrieval, tools, and agents, while keeping the first troubleshooting task manageable.

The original home-lab setup used an Ubuntu virtual machine on Proxmox, 16 virtual CPUs, 16 GB of RAM, Ollama, and Llama 3 with 8 billion parameters. Those are the specifications of that experiment, not a minimum requirement or a performance guarantee for every model.
Establish one working path
Install Ollama using its official instructions for your operating system. Start the service, then download and run the model. These were the core commands in the original experiment:

body.code:
ollama pull llama3
ollama run llama3

children.text: The first command downloads model files. The second opens an interactive session. Ask a small question, wait for the response, and check whether the speed is acceptable before adding a web interface. Model size, quantization, available memory, and CPU or GPU execution all affect the experience.
Keep the model name and runtime version in your notes. When you later change either, you will have a useful baseline for comparing output and latency.
Keep the network boundary explicit

Ollama binds to the loopback interface by default. That is enough when your client and model server run on the same machine. The original article also described connecting from a different computer, but remote access is a separate configuration decision.
The current
Ollama FAQ

documents the host setting and service configuration. Do not expose an inference endpoint publicly just to make a desktop client connect. Decide which machines need access and configure the network accordingly.
Add an interface after inference works
Open WebUI and AnythingLLM were the interfaces considered in the original roadmap. A graphical client can make ongoing conversations easier, but it also adds configuration and storage to understand.

Local inference can work offline after the necessary files are downloaded. Web search, remote tools, cloud models, and application telemetry have their own network behaviour. Check the whole application before describing the complete workflow as offline.
Once the basic conversation works, the next useful experiment is
retrieval over a small local document

title: Local RAG: from documents to answers you can inspect
excerpt: Follow the path from source text to retrieved passages and a local answer, with a clear distinction between embeddings and evidence.

source.title: Local RAG: from documents to answers you can inspect
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies. Clarified that retrieved text, not raw embedding vectors, is supplied to the language model.

children.text: Retrieval-augmented generation adds relevant source material to a model’s input when a question arrives. A local RAG application combines a document collection, an embedding model, a retrieval store, and a language model running on your machine.

The original tutorial built this pipeline with Python, LangChain, Ollama, Llama 3, sentence-transformer embeddings, and SQLiteVSS. Its value is the visible sequence of operations: you can inspect what enters the system, what retrieval selects, and what the model says about it.
Build the document path first

Begin with a small text document. Load it, split it into passages, calculate embeddings, and store those vectors alongside the corresponding text. Keep a link or identifier for the source so a retrieved passage remains traceable.

Chunking is a practical decision. Very short chunks can separate an answer from its context. Very long chunks can dilute the relevant passage or crowd the model’s context window. Inspect a few chunks before treating the configuration as settled.
Inspect retrieval before asking for an answer

Embed the question using the compatible embedding model and run a similarity search. Read the returned passages directly. If they do not contain the answer, fluent generation will not repair the missing evidence.

body.code:
Source document → chunks → embeddings → retrieval store
Question → query embedding → matching passages
Question + matching passages → local language model → answer

children.text: The language model receives retrieved text in its prompt. It does not read the vector database or answer directly from raw embedding vectors. The embeddings help the retriever find candidate passages; the passages provide the evidence.
Make uncertainty observable

A useful application lets readers compare the answer with its sources. Include questions whose answers are present, questions that require more than one passage, and questions the document cannot answer. The last group reveals whether the assistant admits missing information or fills gaps with a plausible story.

The original notebook used a retrieved-context prompt and a question-answering chain. Its package imports describe that historical environment; use the linked source when studying the notebook rather than assuming those imports match today’s libraries.
Once this small pipeline is understandable,
web crawling
can provide another document source. Keep the same inspection points when the input becomes larger or changes more frequently.

title: Llama 3.2 Vision: understanding the local inference workflow
excerpt: A historical walkthrough of image-and-text inference using a vision model, its processor, and a notebook you can inspect.

source.title: Llama 3.2 Vision: understanding the local inference workflow
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: A vision-language model accepts an image together with a text prompt and produces a text response. The original Llama 3.2 Vision experiment used this capability to describe a book cover and explore visual question answering.

That is different from generating an image. It is also different from assuming that a small text-only model can interpret pictures. Model selection needs to match the input and output your application actually requires.
Separate the model from its processor

The notebook downloaded a vision model through Hugging Face and loaded a matching processor. The processor prepared the image and text in the form the model expected. The model then generated tokens, which were decoded into readable text.

body.code:
Image + question
  → matching processor
  → model inputs on the execution device
  → generated tokens
  → decoded text response

children.text: The example used a book-cover image and a request to describe it. Starting with a familiar image makes it easier to notice invented details, missed text, and ambiguous descriptions.
Check access and execution separately

Downloading gated model weights may require accepting the model’s terms and authenticating with Hugging Face. Keep tokens outside committed notebooks. Being able to download weights does not prove that the selected model will fit the available memory.

The original experiment discussed reduced-precision weights and automatic device placement. Its reported memory observations belonged to particular runs. Memory requirements also depend on model variant, image inputs, context length, and runtime configuration.

A notebook running in a hosted service such as Colab is remote execution, even when it uses the same Python libraries as a notebook on your own computer. Distinguish the two when deciding where images may be processed.
Evaluate more than one description

Try a clear photograph, an image with small text, and a picture where the answer is not visible. Compare the output with what the image actually supports. A confident paragraph is not evidence that an object or detail was present.
The source also explored
Clean UI

as an interface for the model. That repository and the recovered notebook document the historical setup. The old claim that other local runtimes could not support Llama 3.2 Vision has been omitted because runtime support changes over time.

title: Web crawling for local RAG: keep the evidence visible
excerpt: Extend a local retrieval pipeline with Crawl4AI, while retaining source URLs and checking what the crawler actually captured.

source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: A local RAG system becomes more useful when its input can include web pages. The original experiment extended a document-based notebook with Crawl4AI, then used the extracted text in the same retrieval and generation pipeline.

The historical stack combined Crawl4AI, LangChain, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, SQLiteVSS, Ollama, and Llama 3 8B. A short Wikipedia page kept the initial example small enough to inspect in a notebook.
Treat crawling as document preparation

Fetching a page and extracting useful text are separate steps. A successful HTTP response can still leave you with navigation, duplicated sections, or missing content. Read the crawler’s output before splitting it into chunks.
Keep the source URL and collection time with the text. When a page changes, that information helps explain why an answer produced from an earlier snapshot differs from what a reader sees today.
Reuse the retrieval pipeline
The original notebook split extracted text, calculated embeddings, stored them in SQLiteVSS, and ran a similarity search. Retrieved passages then became context for a local question-answering prompt.

body.code:
Web page → extracted text → chunks + source metadata
Chunks → embeddings → vector store
Question → relevant passages → local model response

children.text: The retrieval stage selects text; the model reads that text. Adding a crawler does not make every response current or correct. The collection schedule, extraction quality, and retrieval result still determine which evidence reaches the model.
Check failures where they happen

Inspect one example at each boundary: page to text, text to chunks, question to passages, and passages to answer. If an answer is wrong, this makes it possible to locate the failure instead of repeatedly changing the final prompt.

Web content is input data. Instructions found inside it should not gain authority over your application or its tools. For a question that the collected material cannot answer, the useful response is an explicit gap in the evidence.
The recovered article retains the historical notebook steps. For a new implementation, consult
Crawl4AI’s project
for its current installation and extraction interfaces. Start with the
local RAG foundation
if you have not yet verified retrieval over a simple document.

title: MCP with local language models: host, client, server, and tools
excerpt: Understand where the local model sits in an MCP application and how to test a small tool integration before adding more servers.

source.title: MCP with local language models: host, client, server, and tools
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: MCP connects an application to capabilities exposed by servers. A local language model can participate in that application without becoming an MCP server itself. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the first integration easier to understand.
The original experiment used Ollama, Qwen 2.5 7B, and mcp-cli to work with filesystem, search, and fetch capabilities. It explored the practical connection between a local model and external tools.
Put the model in the host application
The host manages the user interaction and model workflow. Its MCP client connects to a server. The server exposes tools or other capabilities and performs the work requested through that connection.
The model can propose a tool call, but application code handles its execution and returns the result. See the
MCP architecture documentation
for the protocol’s separation of responsibilities.
Begin with one narrow capability
The historical setup used a filesystem server configured with a specific directory. That is a useful place to start because you can compare the returned file list with the directory yourself.

Confirm that the client can list the server’s tools before involving the model. Then ask for a simple read operation and inspect both the arguments and returned data. A missing tool connection and a model choosing the wrong tool are different failures.
Tool-calling compatibility depends on the model, runtime, and client. The original article’s broad exclusion of reasoning models is not a reliable rule for selecting a current implementation.
Add remote services deliberately

The experiment then added Brave Search and a fetch server. Those tools communicate over the network even when inference runs locally. Search also introduces a provider credential and its own service requirements.

Adding servers expands the application’s reach. It does not prove that the model will select the correct operation or that every available tool should be exposed in every conversation. Keep credentials outside committed configuration and expose only the capabilities the task needs.
The original client code lives in
mcp-cli
. For a larger example, the
REST API integration series
follows the same pattern through a warehouse service, a local model, and a Python agent.

title: Minion and Minions: testing collaboration between local and cloud models
excerpt: A historical experiment with HazyResearch’s local/cloud model collaboration, and the measurements that make its tradeoffs visible.

source.title: Minion and Minions: testing collaboration between local and cloud models
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: A local model and a cloud model can share a task instead of treating execution as an all-or-nothing choice. HazyResearch’s Minion and Minions work explored that design: local computation contributes to a larger reasoning workflow coordinated with a more capable model.

The original experiment ran the project’s Streamlit application and notebook using Ollama alongside a cloud provider. It compared the two protocols on a document containing hotel information and reservation dialogues.
Follow the information exchanged

The useful question is what each participant sees and produces. A model running locally does not make the combined workflow private if prompts, excerpts, intermediate results, or documents are sent to a cloud service.
The
HazyResearch repository

describes the protocols and their implementation. Minion uses interaction between the models; Minions adds task decomposition and aggregation across local work. Inspect the version you run rather than assuming every variant sends the same information.
Use a question with a known answer

The original task asked for a minibar bill from a longer hotel dialogue. This made it possible to compare the returned value against an identifiable passage instead of judging the answer only by its writing quality.

An interesting intermediate result was that one worker returned a room-rate figure while another found the relevant minibar charge. The aggregation step therefore had to distinguish a superficially relevant amount from the amount that actually answered the question.

That example illustrates why a final correct answer alone is not enough to understand the workflow. Inspect which pieces of evidence were extracted, what the workers misunderstood, and how the final model resolved the difference.
Measure the whole run

Record the model names, input document, protocol settings, requests, tokens, elapsed time, and final answer. The historical runs reported different cloud costs, but one small example is not a general savings estimate.

A stronger comparison includes a direct cloud baseline and questions of different difficulty. Extra coordination may be worthwhile for one workload and unnecessary for another. It also consumes local resources even when the provider bill falls.

Use the linked project for current setup instructions. This edition preserves the experiment’s central lesson: examine the actual exchange of data and work before deciding whether hybrid execution improves your application.

title: OpenAI Agents SDK with a local model: make the workflow explicit
excerpt: A planner-and-writer example that separates local inference, search tools, orchestration, and tracing.

source.title: OpenAI Agents SDK with a local model: make the workflow explicit
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: An agent framework can coordinate work even when the model runs outside the framework provider’s infrastructure. The original experiment connected the OpenAI Agents SDK to an Ollama endpoint and used a planner-and-writer workflow to draft a technical article.

The proposed topic was deploying Apache Ignite with Docker and Kubernetes. The output was intended as a draft to edit and refine, which is an important distinction for any generated technical tutorial.
Configure the model explicitly

An OpenAI-compatible endpoint needs the appropriate base URL, model name, and client configuration. Compatibility is not a promise that every provider feature behaves identically. Tool calling and the selected API interface both matter.
The current
Agents SDK model documentation
explains support for other providers and common compatibility issues. Use it when adapting the historical notebook to a current environment.
Give each step a concrete output

The planner in the example could call a search function to collect relevant material and produce an outline. The writer received the previous step’s output and drafted the article. The surrounding Python workflow connected those stages.

body.code:
Topic → search results → planner’s outline
Outline + source material → writer’s draft
Draft → human review and technical verification

children.text: An agent name or role description does not by itself guarantee a useful handoff. Pass the actual output that the next stage needs, and retain source URLs so a reviewer can check claims.
Account for search and tracing

The notebook wrapped DuckDuckGo search as a callable tool. That search still reaches an external service when the language model runs locally. Model execution and tool execution have different data paths.

Tracing is another independent setting. The SDK can export traces; configure or disable that behaviour according to the environment. A local base URL alone does not establish that the complete workflow stays on the machine.
Treat a technical draft as unfinished work

Review commands against the versions and platform the article names. Check that referenced links support the claims, that prerequisites are complete, and that error paths are explained. A second model can help edit the prose, but it cannot substitute for running the tutorial in its intended environment.
The recovered source contains the original notebook and orchestration examples. For the broader content workflow, continue with
local AI content pipelines

title: A2A in practice: a travel planner with separate agent services
excerpt: Follow a historical weather, search, and local-model example to understand discovery, service boundaries, and task coordination.

source.title: A2A in practice: a travel planner with separate agent services
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: The original A2A experiment built a travel-planning workflow from separate services. One agent fetched weather information, another searched for activities, and a local language model turned the gathered material into a readable plan.

The implementation used the community python-a2a library. Its purpose was to make agent communication tangible through a small example that could be run and inspected, rather than hide every step inside a single prompt.
Separate discovery from orchestration

An Agent Card describes a service’s capabilities and connection information. A client still needs to decide which service to call, send an appropriate request, and handle the result. Publishing a card does not automatically create a reliable planning workflow.

The article also introduced task states and messages. These give the caller a way to represent work in progress, completion, failure, or a request for more input. The exact schema and discovery path belong to the protocol version used by the implementation.
Follow one trip request
The example’s coordinator queried the weather service, used the result to shape a search for indoor or outdoor activities, and sent the gathered information to the local model for summarization.

body.code:
Destination → weather agent
Weather context + destination → search agent
Weather + search results → local model → proposed itinerary

children.text: Weather and search used OpenWeather and Brave APIs. Those calls were remote; local summarization did not make the whole workflow offline. The weather endpoint also needs to match the question: current conditions cannot establish the forecast for a future holiday.
Make partial failure understandable

A useful planner should distinguish a missing weather response from a completed search with no relevant results. Preserve service errors and timestamps rather than letting the final model present incomplete data as a fully supported itinerary.

The historical weather example logged request details. When adapting it, redact credentials from URLs and logs. Authentication support in a protocol does not configure or secure the deployed services on its own.
Keep tools and agents in perspective

MCP and A2A address different integration boundaries: accessing exposed capabilities and communicating with agent services. Neither removes the application’s responsibility to coordinate work or validate results.
The author’s
tutorial code
preserves the example. Credit also belongs to
python-a2a
and its contributors. This is an edited account of the 2025 implementation, not a claim of conformance with a newer protocol release.

title: Local AI content pipelines: build a reviewable draft, then publish
excerpt: Use local models to structure research, drafting, and editing without confusing generated volume with useful technical content.

source.title: Local AI content pipelines: build a reviewable draft, then publish
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies. Removed promises of effortless income, zero cost, and automatic publication quality.

children.text: A useful content pipeline starts with a deliverable somebody needs: an API guide, a developer onboarding page, a lab exercise, or a clearer explanation of an internal system. Local models can help prepare those materials, but the value comes from their accuracy and usefulness.

The original article proposed a workflow using Ollama and CrewAI, with roles for research, writing, editing, and optional quality review. It also explored delivering the result as Markdown, HTML, or a document.
Define the input before assigning roles

For a technical guide, provide the relevant repository, documentation, supported versions, intended reader, and expected outcome. A writer supplied only with a topic has to fill far more gaps than one working from a specific source package.
Keep research notes and source links alongside the draft. An editor should be able to distinguish a documented fact from an assumption or a suggestion introduced during generation.
Give each stage a useful handoff

The researcher gathers relevant material. The planner turns that material into an outline. The writer develops the explanation. The editor improves clarity and consistency. A technical reviewer checks the instructions against the actual system.

body.code:
Source package → evidence notes → outline → draft
Draft → editorial review → technical verification → publication

children.text: More agents are not automatically better. Start with the fewest stages that make the work easier to inspect. Add a stage when it addresses a recurring problem, such as missing prerequisites or unsupported claims.
Understand the local tradeoff

Running inference locally can avoid a model API charge, but hardware, electricity, maintenance, and review time still have costs. Search tools and hosted integrations may also communicate outside the machine.

The original article described several possible commercial uses, including documentation services and educational material. These are potential delivery models, not evidence that generated content will earn revenue. A reader still needs a reason to trust and use the result.
Publish after the work is checked

For a tutorial, execute the commands in the environment it names. For an architecture explanation, compare the description with the implementation. For an onboarding guide, ask whether a new reader can reach the stated outcome without filling in undocumented steps.
The accompanying
book repository
includes the broader examples behind this workflow. The
Agents SDK edition
shows another way to coordinate a planner and writer. Choose the framework around the handoffs you need to observe and maintain.

title: MCP and REST APIs, part 1: expose warehouse operations as tools
excerpt: Build the service boundary first: FastAPI operations, Redis data, MCP tools, and direct inspection before adding a model.

source.title: MCP and REST APIs, part 1: expose warehouse operations as tools
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: An existing application already knows how to validate and perform its business operations. An MCP integration can expose selected operations to an AI application while keeping that service boundary in place.

The first part of this series built a small warehouse-order API with FastAPI and Redis, then connected it to an MCP server using fastapi-mcp. The exercise made it possible to compare a conventional API request with an invocation through an MCP client.
Start with operations you can test directly

The service created, retrieved, listed, updated, and deleted orders. Each order included an identifier, a customer name, items, and a status. Redis hashes held the order data, with a set tracking order identifiers and a counter supplying new IDs.

body.code:
POST   /orders             create an order
GET    /orders             list orders
GET    /orders/{order_id}  retrieve an order
PUT    /orders/{order_id}  update an order
DELETE /orders/{order_id}  delete an order

children.text: Test those operations through the API before adding a model. A tool wrapper cannot repair incorrect validation or an inconsistent data update. The storage example also needs an explicit persistence configuration if data must survive a Redis restart.
Expose a deliberate tool surface

The integration mapped API operations into MCP tools. This gives a client structured descriptions and inputs to work with; it does not make every generated argument valid or every available operation appropriate for every user.

In this example, the application layer is a useful place to retain business rules. That is a design choice for the warehouse service, not a claim that every database-backed MCP server must use a REST intermediary.
Inspect the MCP connection independently

The original walkthrough used MCP Inspector to list tools and invoke a read operation. That separates server connectivity from model behaviour. Compare the result with a direct request to the API before trying natural-language interaction.
The historical setup used SSE and an MCP endpoint mounted on the FastAPI application. Transport and mounting APIs vary by library version, so consult the
original project files
when studying that implementation.
Adding MCP does not supply authorization automatically. Decide who may read or modify an order at the service boundary. In
part 2
, the same tools are connected to a local model;
part 3
moves the workflow into a Python agent.

title: MCP and REST APIs, part 2: connect a local model to the service
excerpt: Connect Ollama and mcp-cli to the warehouse example, then separate tool discovery from correct execution.

source.title: MCP and REST APIs, part 2: connect a local model to the service
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: With the warehouse API and MCP server working, the next step is to place a local model in the loop. The second part of the series used Ollama and mcp-cli to translate natural-language requests into calls to the exposed tools.
The original experiment used a tool-capable model such as Qwen 2.5. Choosing a model that can chat is not enough to establish that it supports the tool-calling interface required by the client.
Verify discovery before interpretation

Start the API and its backing Redis instance. Configure the MCP client to reach the server, start local inference, and inspect the available tool list. In the historical client, the chat command /tools displayed those capabilities.

Then ask for all warehouse orders. Compare the returned records with a direct API query. Follow with a narrower request, such as listing orders in a pending state. These checks reveal whether the model selected a suitable tool and interpreted its result correctly.
Treat writes as a separate capability

The original demonstration also included deleting an order by customer name. A name can match more than one record, so a dependable application should resolve the intended order IDs before performing the operation.

For an illustrative cancellation flow, first retrieve candidate orders, display their identifiers and statuses, and obtain confirmation for the specific records to change. The service must still enforce the caller’s permissions. A persuasive natural-language request does not replace that boundary.
Understand the container network

The article packaged FastAPI and Redis in Docker Compose. Inside that Compose network, the application addressed Redis using its service hostname. A model server running on the host is a different connection and needs its own reachable address.

body.code: Local model ↔ MCP client ↔ MCP server / FastAPI ↔ Redis

children.text: Keep each connection independently testable. If the database is unavailable, inspect the API-to-Redis path. If no tools appear, inspect the MCP connection. If the wrong tool is chosen, examine the model interaction and tool descriptions.
The
original FastAPI files
and
mcp-cli project
document the historical setup. Local inference gives control over where model requests run; it does not by itself establish reliability or privacy for every connected component.
Continue to
part 3
to make this interaction an explicit Python workflow, or revisit the
service foundation

title: MCP and REST APIs, part 3: build an inspectable Python agent
excerpt: Use mcp-agent to connect tool discovery, local inference, and a warehouse summary without hiding the application’s responsibilities.

source.title: MCP and REST APIs, part 3: build an inspectable Python agent
source.editorialNote: Republished with permission as a condensed, edited edition. The original date comes from the QuickStart archive; the full text was recovered from the author’s own site. Historical examples have not been rerun against current dependencies.

children.text: The final part of the warehouse series moved from an interactive client to a Python workflow. It used the mcp-agent framework to connect to the MCP server, attach a local model, query inventory information, and summarize the result.
The earlier layers remained in place: FastAPI performed warehouse operations and Redis stored order data. The agent coordinated calls to that service rather than accessing the database directly.
Keep the runtime configuration visible

The historical configuration named the MCP server, configured its connection, and selected an OpenAI-compatible Ollama endpoint for inference. The example used Qwen 2.5 and a framework wrapper for the model interaction.

A server name in configuration is a reference the application uses to locate a connection. The MCP client discovers exposed tools through MCP. The FastAPI integration may derive those tools from API definitions, but the client is not independently discovering arbitrary REST endpoints.
Make the workflow observable

The example initialized an MCPApp, created an inventory agent, listed available tools, attached the model wrapper, and issued prompts. A follow-up prompt requested a summary of the gathered information.

body.code:
Initialize runtime → connect server → inspect tools
Attach model → request inventory data → inspect result → summarize

children.text: These are useful boundaries for logging and debugging. A model response should remain connected to the tool results that support it. Avoid logging credentials or unnecessary customer information while making those boundaries observable.
Decide what happens between runs

The original article proposed persistent memory as an extension. That raises concrete questions: which state belongs to a task, how long it should be retained, and whether a later run may rely on an earlier inventory snapshot.
A summary can become stale when orders change. Retained conversation history should not silently replace a fresh service query when the user asks for the current state.
Carry service rules into the agent workflow

Useful extensions include clearer tool descriptions, bounded retries, explicit handling of partial results, and authorization on the service. None is supplied merely by attaching a model or choosing an asynchronous runtime.
The
author’s agent example
and
mcp-agent project
preserve the implementation. Start with
part 1
for the API design and
part 2
for the interactive local-model connection. Together, the three layers show where each responsibility belongs and where a failure can be inspected.

title: Better AI agents show their work
excerpt: Why editable intermediate work can make an AI assistant easier to guide, verify, and improve.

source.title: Your AI Is a Caged Genius — Here’s How to Set It Free
source.editorialNote: Edited from Timur’s essay, first listed on QuickStart on 27 June 2025 and republished by Ardor on 12 July 2025. Condensed to its central design argument; unsupported statistics, speed promises, and absolute safety claims have been removed. MCP terminology has been corrected.

children.text: An assistant becomes easier to collaborate with when it exposes the work between a request and its answer. A query, a small script, or a visible set of source records gives the user something concrete to inspect and correct.

The original essay illustrated this with a project-status report assembled from several workplace tools. If the assistant selects the wrong channel or date range, a visible intermediate step lets the user identify the mistake before accepting the summary.
Make correction part of the interface

The design argument is straightforward: show which information was used and how it was transformed. Let the user revise an assumption and continue from that point. Treat example scenarios as illustrations, not measured productivity results.
Keep capability and control together

MCP means Model Context Protocol. It does not require a fixed linear workflow, and code execution can complement exposed tools. Neither approach removes the need for scoped permissions and review of consequential operations.

An isolated execution environment can reduce risk, but it cannot guarantee harmless behaviour. The useful goal is an assistant whose actions and intermediate results remain understandable enough for a person to guide and verify.

title: From Copilot to Colleague: the book and how I built it
excerpt: A ten-chapter book on AI engineering, built from 794 practitioner talks, where every claim points to the exact moment it came from.

source.title: From Copilot to Colleague
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from the book’s public README and method notes. Figures and claims come from those documents.

children.text: I built a book. It is called *From Copilot to Colleague: How AI Engineering Turns Models into Dependable Systems*. You can read it online at
fromcopilottocolleague.com

It is also a public experiment. The question was whether autonomous research loops, working from a real corpus, can produce a source-anchored book on AI engineering. The loops drafted the manuscript. The repository holds the method that produced it.
The book has one thesis. Models create possibility. Scaffolding creates trust. Organizations decide whether that trust compounds. The ten chapters are the argument for that line.
What the book covers

The book has ten chapters in four acts. The first act, chapters 1 and 2, states the problem. AI is moving from answering questions to doing delegated work, and cheap generation makes human judgment more visible, not less.

The second act, chapters 3 to 7, builds the scaffolding stack. It covers harnesses and specs that agents can use, evals as a control system, context as infrastructure, runtimes with a human control plane, and security and identity for systems that act.

The third act, chapter 8, is the stress test. Realtime voice removes the hiding places that text chat gives a weak system. The last act, chapters 9 and 10, widens the view. It asks what an AI-native organization looks like and which ideas endure when the tools change.
Where the material comes from
An AI-drafted book with no source of truth only remixes what the model already knows. I wanted a source of truth. The corpus is 794 talks from practitioners on the AI Engineer YouTube channel.

The rule of the project is simple: no anchor, no claim. Every claim in the manuscript carries a video, a start and end time, and a verbatim quote. The website shows these under each chapter, so a reader can jump to the exact moment in the talk.
How the quality is checked

No single model should grade prose shaped like its own output. A panel of three AI models from different families scores each chapter on six dimensions: humanness, voice, usefulness, evidence density, claim defensibility, and redundancy. The median score is the verdict. When the three models disagree by more than 20 points, that cell is flagged as the place to look.

The repository holds the whole method: the agent instructions, the research passes, and the judges. A bounded research loop takes one mission at a time, commits its result, and logs the pass. Every step is reversible and sits in git.
What I will post here

The book is the proof that the method works. The method is the deliverable. Over the next posts I will go through the book chapter by chapter. Each chapter gets three short posts: its core argument, a practical way to apply it this week, and one scene or example that teaches a single lesson.
Start where your own work hurts. If agents disappoint you, read about harnesses. If you cannot tell whether a change made things better, read about evals. If you ship to real users, read about trust.
This post draws on the whole of
From Copilot to Colleague

title: AI engineering starts when answers become delegated work
excerpt: Chapter 1 argues the hard problem in AI is no longer better answers. It is trusting a system that comes back with work done.

source.title: Chapter 1 — The Shift: From Assistant to Delegate
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 1 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: For a while, the most impressive thing AI could do was answer. It answered faster than search and more fluently than documentation. That changed user expectations and product design. It did not yet change the nature of work.

The change begins when we ask the system to return with work done. Research this market and come back with a memo. Refactor this service, run the checks, and prepare the patch for review. Chapter 1 argues that this is a different standard, and that most of AI engineering follows from it.
A different kind of failure

A helpful answer can be wrong and still be useful. Delegated work costs more. It consumes time, touches systems, and shapes decisions. It also hides its mistakes inside output that looks plausible enough to pass a casual glance.

The book says that the primary failure surface is not the work that looks broken. It is the work that looks finished. A test claimed to pass, a source claimed to be checked, a step claimed to be done: the same shape of failure appears wherever an agent reports on its own success. So the question moves from "is the answer good?" to "can we verify the work by something other than the system's own account of itself?"
Three roles and one test

The book separates three kinds of system. An assistant suggests. A copilot collaborates inside a tight human loop. A delegate is given a unit of work and is expected to come back with an artifact, a recommendation, or a completed step. The labels matter less than where the human sits. With an assistant, nothing takes effect until you read it. With a delegate, you step out of the moment-to-moment loop and back in at review.

I offer one quick test. Ask what happens if no human looks at the output for the next 24 hours. An assistant's suggestion goes stale, which is harmless. A delegate's output has usually already changed something: a pull request opened, a record updated, a deadline running that someone else now inherits. If your system fails that test the delegate way, you are past the assistant stage, whatever the product page says.
Trust under action

Joel Hron puts the shift cleanly: the north star has moved "from helpfulness to productive." Once a system acts for users, prompt cleverness stops being the central problem. Trust under action takes its place.

That is why I define AI engineering as the discipline of turning raw model capability into delegated work that can be structured, measured, supervised, and trusted. Prompting, retrieval, evals, workflow engines, guardrails, observability, and approval systems often look like separate subcultures. In the book they are pieces of one discipline. Each answers the same question: what must surround intelligence before it is safe to delegate work to it?

The chapter also takes a position on autonomy. The goal is not maximum agency in every direction. In many valuable systems the right design is adjustable autonomy. Let the machine move fast where the risk is low and the checks are strong. Slow it down where consequences are harder to reverse.

Here is the takeaway to try this week. Pick one AI feature your team runs or plans to ship and apply the 24-hour test. Write down what changes in the world if nobody reads its output for a day. If the answer is "something," treat the feature as a delegate. That means giving it the structure, measurement, and review points you would give any colleague whose work others will rely on.

From Copilot to Colleague

title: Five checks to run before you delegate work to an AI
excerpt: Turn the Chapter 1 checklist into a week of small, concrete steps that show whether your AI system is ready to take on delegated work.

source.title: Chapter 1 — The Shift: From Assistant to Delegate
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 1 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 1 of my book ends with a practical checklist. It has five items. None needs new tooling. This post turns them into steps a team can take in one week.
Monday: classify what you are building

Start with the 24-hour test. Ask what happens if no human reads the output for a day. If nothing changes in the world, you have an assistant. If a pull request opens, a record updates, or a clock starts running, you have a delegate.
Write the answer next to the feature name. The label matters because it sets the rigor. The book says to treat a delegate with delegate-grade rigor, whatever the product page calls it.
Tuesday: test for dependability, not for a demo
Pick one task. Phrase the same request three different ways. Run all three with no one watching closely. Compare the results.

A demo only has to clear the bar once. A production system has to clear it every time, unobserved. If the behavior drifts across the three runs, the system is not ready to delegate to yet. The book says that this holds no matter how good the single showcase run looked.
Wednesday: verify from outside

Find every step where your only evidence is the agent saying it happened. Then replace that evidence with something else: a test result you run yourself, a link to the actual source, a record in the system of record.

Rafael Levi at Bright Data describes why. Web-browsing agents that hit a block do not say so: "There's no error, no warning, just the wrong answer." The checklist puts it in one line. If the only evidence a step happened is the agent saying so, you have no evidence.
Thursday: write the standard down
Ask a senior engineer for three conventions that live only in their head. Local naming rules, dependency habits, and rollback instincts are common examples. Put them in a file the agent can read.
The chapter's rule is that a standard has to be made explicit before it can be delegated, or it will be violated silently. The system cannot inherit what the organization never wrote down.
Friday: name the missing piece

Walk through the seven things a trustworthy delegate needs. They are the right context, usable tools, explicit constraints, evaluation loops, durable state, approval boundaries, and observability. For your system, mark each one as present, partial, or missing.

Then name the one that hurts most. The chapter asks teams to do this before blaming the model for a failure. The book argues that a missing layer is usually where the workflow fails first. A serious agent product with no trace view or approval queue has a reliability gap, not a leaner design.
What you have by Friday

After five short sessions you hold a classification, a drift test result, a list of unverified claims, a standards file, and a ranked gap. That is a small plan for making delegated work trustworthy, built from the evidence of your own system.
If you only have time for one step, pick Wednesday. Verification by something other than the system's own account is the habit that makes the other four useful.
