title: Meridian's coding agent worked until the scope grew
excerpt: A composite fintech case from Chapter 1 shows why erratic agent quality often points to the workplace, not the model.

source.title: Chapter 1 — The Shift: From Assistant to Delegate
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 1 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Two composite cases run through my book. They are drawn from real patterns, not from a single company. The first appears in Chapter 1 and returns later. I call it the Software Factory, and it is anchored in a company I named Meridian.

Meridian is a mid-size fintech. It starts with an ordinary payments repository and a strong coding model. At first the agent feels magical on small tasks. Then the team expands scope, and quality gets erratic.
The easy conclusion
Many teams reach for the same explanation at this point: the model is not good enough. They wait for a better one or try a different one.

The case pushes against that reflex. The model is not always the real problem. The deeper issue at Meridian is that the workplace was never made legible enough for delegated machine work. A small task fits inside what the model can see. A larger one depends on things nobody wrote down.
What was hidden

The chapter explains what those things are. Delegation exposes how much good work always depended on tacit human judgment. In a software setting, that means local conventions, architecture taste, dependency discipline, rollback instinct, performance habits, and many non-functional expectations that senior engineers carry in their heads.

Strong teams internalize this so thoroughly that they mistake it for natural background competence. Then they hand the work to a machine collaborator, and the hidden standards become a liability. The system cannot reliably inherit what the organization never externalized.
What Meridian does about it

The team adds harnesses, specs, validation, context discipline, eval loops, runtime structure, and review surfaces. A harness, in the book's usage, is the structure around a coding agent that makes its work bounded and inspectable. As the team builds these, the repository changes character. It starts behaving less like a chat playground and more like a managed production environment for machine labor.

I use this case to show how quickly "AI coding" stops being a prompt problem and becomes a systems problem. Nothing in Meridian's story requires a smarter model. It requires a workplace that a delegate can read.
A second case, briefly

The second case, a tax and advisory firm I called Hargrove, follows the same path with different stakes. Its assistant starts as a conversational surface and then gets asked to do professional work. Fluency is no longer enough. In both cases the book says that the more valuable the delegated work becomes, the more the surrounding system matters.
The lesson to take

When an agent does well on small tasks and erratically on larger ones, check the workplace before you check the model. Ask what a new colleague would need to know to do this work well, and whether any of it exists outside someone's head.

You can run this as a short exercise. Pick the last task where the agent's output disappointed you. List the unwritten expectations that the output violated. Each item on that list is a candidate for a spec, a validation, or a repo rule. The book's practical rule applies here: make the standard explicit before you delegate it, or it will be violated silently.

title: When code gets cheap, judgment gets expensive
excerpt: Chapter 2 argues that cheap generation does not remove the human contribution. It makes taste, the ability to tell good from convincing, easier to see.

source.title: Chapter 2 — Taste Still Matters When Code Gets Cheap
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 2 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A team can now generate ten versions of a feature instead of one. A founder can build a prototype in a weekend. A junior engineer can land patches that once took far longer. Some of this is real. Routine output has become cheaper.

Chapter 2 makes the case that cheap output does not mean cheap judgment. The bottleneck shifts toward deciding what should exist, what quality looks like, which tradeoffs are acceptable, and what to reject. The human contribution does not disappear. It becomes easier to see.
Why fundamentals matter more

Matt Pocock says "software fundamentals matter now more than they actually ever have." That can sound backward. If a model fills in the syntax, scaffolds the endpoint, and drafts the tests, surely fundamentals matter less.

The chapter's answer is that fundamentals were never about syntax. They are how you tell good output from merely convincing output. Which abstraction belongs here? Which dependency will quietly punish us six months from now? Which draft only looks polished because nobody asked whether the premise is right? A machine cannot resolve these for you.

These decisions always mattered. What changes is their visibility. In a slower workflow, production was expensive, so teams moved slower, touched fewer surfaces, and got incidental review for free. Cheap generation strips away that natural throttle. You can now build a much larger amount of work on top of weak decisions.
Taste as a working definition

I define taste as quality discrimination under abundance. It is the ability to notice the difference between output that merely works and output that fits. The tells are specific. A patch is technically correct but shaped wrong for the system around it. A component boundary is too clever. A prototype convenience is about to become permanent structure. None of these trip a test.

Tuomas Artman, speaking with Gergely Orosz about craft at Linear, asks: "What happens when agents are capable of doing everything immediately for you?" The obvious answer is speed. Artman's answer, as I summarize it in the book, is sharper. When a small AI-equipped team can match your feature set, tasteful, high-quality software is a way to keep some competitive advantage.
An amplifier, not a replacement

This is why I describe AI as an amplifier before it is a replacement. Good operators get more leverage. Sloppy operators get more slop, faster. If a team has strong standards, explicit constraints, and people who discriminate well, the new speed is extraordinary. If it lacks them, the same speed means it can industrialize confusion.

The scarce skill is therefore less often the manual act of producing. It is more often selecting, directing, constraining, sequencing, and refusing. The chapter's closing move says the question to ask is not what happens to programmers but what happens to standards.

The takeaway is a small one. This week, pick one place where your team accepted generated work because it looked finished. Ask what standard would have told you whether it fit. If you cannot state that standard in a sentence, you have found the real gap. Write the sentence down, and put it where the next reviewer and the next model can both read it.

title: A week-long plan to keep taste in your AI workflow
excerpt: Five habits from the Chapter 2 checklist, laid out as steps a team can start this week to protect quality as generation gets cheap.

source.title: Chapter 2 — Taste Still Matters When Code Gets Cheap
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 2 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 2 of my book argues that cheap generation raises the value of judgment. The chapter ends with a practical checklist of five habits. Here is how a team can start each one this week.
Run the framing gate before you delegate

Sean Grove at OpenAI says the new scarce skill is "writing specifications that fully capture the intent." I turn this into a gate. Before you hand anything to a model, answer five questions in writing. What is the actual task? What counts as success? Which constraints are real? What may stay rough? What would make the result unacceptable even if it looks finished?
Treat the last question as the test. If you cannot answer it, you are not ready to delegate. In the chapter's words, with these questions unanswered you do not have a task, you have a prompt.
Read every diff like its author
When you wrote every line, comprehension came free with authorship. A model breaks that bundle. It hands you working code you did not build, and you now pay for understanding separately.

So read the diff the way an author would. Reconstruct why each choice was made, rather than confirming the lines parse. Then trace one path the tests do not cover and ask whether the design survives it. Make this a visible step in your review, with a named person responsible.
Sort your friction before you cut it

Ronacher and Poncela Cubeiro argue in *The Friction Is Your Judgment* that some friction is judgment in disguise. I offer a simple sort. Cut a pause if removing it only costs keystrokes, such as boilerplate, glue, or scaffolding the model can regenerate on demand. Keep a pause if removing it costs a decision, such as whether the architecture can carry this change or whether the draft is right or merely plausible.
List your team's pauses on one page. Mark each as keystrokes or decisions. Protect the second group.
Know which mode you are in

Vibe coding is intuition-led building with low spec and high speed. The chapter calls it a mode, not a production philosophy. It suits discovery, where being wrong is cheap. Once an artifact has to be maintained by someone who did not prompt it into being, switch modes.
Add a line to your project README or ticket template that names the mode. "Exploration" and "has to endure" are enough. The label makes the switch a deliberate act.
Write your constraints down

Taste kept only in a senior engineer's head is easy to lose in delegation. Taste written into a harness, a spec, or a repo rule is harder to lose. A harness here means the structure around a coding agent that tells it how to work.

Start with five rules your reviewers repeat most often. Write each as a sentence an agent could follow. A team that states its standards explicitly can delegate more safely than one that relies on vibe and shared memory.
A rule of thumb to keep

I included one line of my own in the chapter: when generation outruns review, the loop is not fast, it is unreviewed. Use that as your check at the end of the week. If your team produced more this week than it could carefully read, the habits above need more room, not less.

title: The Friday app and the Monday rewrite
excerpt: Corey Gallon's vibe-coding hangover, quoted in Chapter 2, shows when a fast exploratory build has outlived its usefulness.

source.title: Chapter 2 — Taste Still Matters When Code Gets Cheap
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 2 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 2 of my book includes a short scene that many builders will recognize. Corey Gallon at Rexmore calls it the vibe-coding hangover. The app works on Friday. Then, in his words, "Monday rolls around, you want to add a feature… and you realize that you don't understand it, you can't maintain it, and you have to throw most or all of it away."
I keep returning to this scene because it contains a precise lesson about when speed stops paying.
The mode is fine

Vibe coding is low-spec, high-speed, intuition-led building steered by momentum rather than explicit structure. I do not treat it as worthless. The chapter says it can be brilliant. For exploration, interface sketching, rough prototypes, internal tooling, and one-off automation, it can be the correct move. It makes experimentation cheap enough that more people discover what is worth building.
The book says that vibe coding is not the enemy. Unexamined vibe coding is. A mode that works for discovery becomes a problem when it quietly hardens into a default production philosophy.
What Monday reveals

Look at what changes between Friday and Monday in Gallon's account. The app has not broken. It still works. What has changed is the demand on it: it now has to change, and nobody understands it well enough to change it safely.

That is the tell I describe in the chapter. Nobody stood in the way of the build, and nothing failed a test. The cost was deferred until someone needed the code to be maintainable. Production work pays that bill. Chris Kelly at Augment Code makes the same point from the other side. AI code is still code, and vibes do not cut it in production. It still has to live somewhere, interact with systems and users, and be read by future maintainers. The machine does not repeal software reality.
One switch

The chapter reduces mode awareness to a single switch. Use vibe coding where the cost of being wrong is low and the goal is discovery. Leave it behind the moment the output has to endure. If the Monday that Gallon describes is coming, the exploratory mode has already outlived its usefulness.

For genuinely disposable work, such as a one-off script or a prototype nobody inherits, I say skip the judgment overhead. The point is not to slow every build down. It is to know which kind of build you are doing.
The takeaway

Before you start a build with a model, say aloud which mode it is. If the answer is exploration, set a condition for review: the moment someone other than the author has to maintain the result, the mode changes. At that point, write the spec you skipped, state the constraints, and read the code like its author would.

You can also run this as a check on work already in flight. Pick one app or script built mostly by momentum. Ask whether someone who did not prompt it into being would have to change it next month. If yes, you are on the Friday side of Gallon's story. Make the switch now, not on Monday.

title: Blame the workplace before you blame the model
excerpt: When coding agents disappoint, the cause is often a repository nobody made legible. Chapter 3 argues the harness matters before the model does.

source.title: Chapter 3 — Harnesses, Specs, and Codebases Agents Can Actually Use
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 3 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: When a coding agent disappoints, teams reach for the same explanation. The model missed a dependency. The model misread the architecture. The model broke a convention nobody told it about. In the postmortem, intelligence becomes the default suspect.

Chapter 3 argues that this diagnosis is often too flattering to the humans involved. Sometimes the model really is not capable enough. But in production codebases, many failures point somewhere else. The environment was never made legible enough for delegated work.
The harness is the interface

Ryan Lopopolo puts it bluntly: "The important thing is not the code but the prompt and the guardrails that got you there." Once a machine does implementation work, its surroundings become part of the product. The book calls those surroundings the harness. The harness is the repository, the specs, the validations, and the workflow that decide what kind of work an agent can do.

Chat tools hide this. You type a request and wait for a patch, so the prompt looks like the whole interface. It is only the visible tip. The real interface is the codebase plus the setup instructions, naming conventions, tests, lint rules, examples of good patches, ADRs, and the performance or security rules that no single file states. A human engineer absorbs these slowly by asking teammates. An agent gets no apprenticeship unless the team builds one.
Slop is a missing standard

Good code carries many unstated decisions: tone, proportion, dependency choices, rollback safety, test shape. Lopopolo says one patch can require "500 little decisions" around underspecified non-functional requirements. I do not treat the number as exact. The point is density. A human fills those gaps with craft and context. An agent fills them by inference. Lopopolo notes that models have seen "trillions of lines of code that make every possible choice of those non-functional requirements that you could ever imagine." Leave a requirement unspecified and the agent samples one of those choices. Nothing makes the sample yours.

So slop is often not the sign of a weak model. It is the sign of a task whose success criteria were never written down. The rule underneath is hard: a standard that lives only in scattered memory is one the agent cannot inherit, and will therefore break.

That changes the prescription. Prompting better helps a little. Reducing the silent guesswork the environment demands helps more. Externalize architecture choices. Store examples of accepted patterns. Make non-functional constraints explicit. The book calls this harness engineering: the systematic conversion of tacit engineering judgment into durable, machine-usable constraints.
What to take from it

A capable model in a murky repository resembles a strong engineer who joins a company with no onboarding and no record of past decisions. You may get lucky. You cannot count on it. The benefit also reaches past agents. New hires and future maintainers gain from the same legibility, because the agent only exposes the difference between standards a team possesses and standards it can operationalize.

My takeaway is small and concrete. Pick one standard your senior engineers enforce in review but have never written down. Put it where an agent can read it: a lint rule, a checked-in example, or a line in a spec. Then watch whether the next patch respects it. If it does, you have moved one piece of judgment out of a person's head and into the codebase.

excerpt: A practical plan from Chapter 3. Five steps a team can start this week to turn a repository into a place where a coding agent can work.

source.title: Chapter 3 — Harnesses, Specs, and Codebases Agents Can Actually Use
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 3 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 3 of my book makes one claim: if you want AI to write production software, start with the environment, not the model. The environment is the harness. It covers your repository, specs, validations, and workflow. Here are five steps from the chapter's checklist that a team can start this week.
Test the repo and fix the spec

First, run the fresh-container test. Clone the repo into a clean environment. Time how long an agent takes to reach a green test run. Every step that lives in someone's shell history is a hole. The agent will fill that hole by guessing. Write the step into a setup script, and run the test again until the agent gets there without help.

Second, watch for repeated hand-patching. If you keep fixing the same kind of mistake in the output, stop fixing the output. Al Harris says "the spec then becomes the natural language representation of your system." Treat it that way. Find the line in the spec that under-specified the work, change it, and regenerate. Repeated correction is the signal that intent belongs in a persistent artifact the next run will read. The operational test is simple. Would the intent survive a fresh agent picking up the task cold? If not, it does not belong only in the prompt.

Third, size the spec to the cost of being wrong. Not every ticket needs a design doc. Over-specification can turn exploration into bureaucracy. I suggest saving the ceremony for work that is large, parallelized, safety-sensitive, or expensive to review. Let everything else move fast.
Hold back the fan-out

Fourth, do not run many agents until one agent succeeds alone, nearly every time. Eno Reyes is explicit on this point. You cannot fan out parallel agents until single-task execution succeeds nearly 100 percent of the time. If you cannot tell automatically whether one change is safe, running twenty only multiplies unverified output. The validation you have sets the ceiling on how much you can delegate.

Reyes also sets a low bar on purpose: "a slop test is better than no test." A rough check is a start. Once it exists, the next agent follows it, and the rules ratchet tighter. You can even ask a coding agent to find where your linters are not opinionated enough, and have it write the missing rule.
Audit the list and fix the first gap

Fifth, audit your actual repo against the agent-readiness list in the chapter. Check for a stable folder structure. Check for explicit setup, build, and run commands. Check for type, lint, and test gates the agent can run repeatedly. Check that architecture decisions live in files, that examples of accepted patterns exist for tests, APIs, migrations, and reviews, that specs sit close enough to the work to survive handoff, and that narrow scripts cover common operations.

Then fix the first item that is missing. Do not fix the easiest one. The chapter is clear that each skipped item is a place where the agent will guess, so the first gap you find is the first place a guess will hurt you.

None of this is glamorous. That is why it works. The chapter argues that the biggest gains in coding agents often come from removing avoidable ambiguity in the repository, not from clever prompting. Reyes puts a number on it: this is where "the real like 5x, 6x, 7x comes from," and "it's a choice that you as an organization have."
Start with the fresh-container test on Monday. By Friday you will know which of your team's standards were written down and which lived only in people's heads.

source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 3 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 3 follows a fictional payments team called Meridian. They start where many teams start: a good model inside an ordinary repository. At first the results feel magical. Then the team widens the scope, and quality turns erratic. One Tuesday shows why.
The diff that looked clean

A senior engineer hands the agent a migration. Move three endpoints onto the new state machine, and keep the house style. The agent comes back in minutes with a clean-looking diff. It compiles. The tests pass.

But the diff pulls in a parsing dependency the team had quietly banned. It also batches writes inside a loop. That is exactly the pattern a payments incident taught the team to avoid six months earlier. Neither rule was written anywhere the agent could read.
The review does not save them. The reviewer catches the dependency, misses the write pattern, and approves. The convention resurfaces later in a review comment nobody will search again.
The agent guessed

The team could say the model is inconsistent. The chapter says what they really mean is that the workplace is inconsistent. None of this was a hallucination. The agent guessed because the workplace gave it nothing firmer to stand on.

This is the lesson I want to keep from the scene. Good code carries many unstated decisions, and the agent fills each gap by inference. Lopopolo, whom I quote in the chapter, says the models have seen "trillions of lines of code that make every possible choice of those non-functional requirements that you could ever imagine." When your requirement is unwritten, the agent picks one of those choices. Nothing makes the pick yours.

It also shows how a human reviewer can fail in the same place. The ban on the dependency was easy to remember. The write pattern lived in memory from an incident. A standard that exists only in scattered memory is one an agent cannot inherit, and one a reviewer can miss.
The unglamorous morning

The next morning the team does plain work. They check in an example of an accepted migration. They add a lint rule for the banned import. They write a setup script that ends the Slack archaeology. They also add agent-facing instructions and tighter lint and type gates.

Nothing in that list needs a better model. The repo becomes less like a haunted archive of past decisions and more like a managed surface for machine labor. The chapter calls the larger pattern a Software Factory: a repository run as a staged, inspectable production line for delegated work. The leverage sits where the team stopped treating its own tacit judgment as invisible infrastructure.

I would add one practical note. Look at the two rules in this scene. One became a lint rule, which a machine can enforce. The other needs a checked-in example, which shows the pattern. Different rules need different forms. The point is that each one ends up somewhere the agent can reach.

So take your last painful review comment, the one that began "we never do it this way here." Ask where an agent would find that rule. If the answer is nowhere, turn it into a lint rule or an example before the next delegated task.

title: A working demo is not a control loop
excerpt: Models look right often enough that teams stop measuring. Chapter 4 argues that evals are the control system that makes delegation safe to trust.

source.title: Chapter 4 — Evals Are the Control System
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 4 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: The first failure mode of AI systems is obvious. They can be wrong. The second is more dangerous. They can look right often enough that teams stop measuring.

A demo works twice in a row. A prototype returns a plausible answer. A coding agent lands a decent patch in a familiar repo. Soon everyone speaks in the language of vibes. Ido Pesok captures the moment with a line every team knows: "It worked first try... I even tested it twice... So from there we're good to ship, right?"
Chapter 4 argues that the demo was not fake. The problem is that a successful demo is not yet a control loop.
What evals are for

People often misread the role of evals. They are not there to decorate a launch deck or to compare two models in the abstract. They create a feedback system around delegated work. As tasks grow from single-line completion to repo-scale changes and multi-step workflows, the gap between toy metrics and operational reliability widens. The question changes. It stops being "Is the model smart?" It becomes "Can this system repeatedly do useful work in our environment without silently drifting out of bounds?"

For that reason The chapter asks readers to stop treating evals as a one-time gate. Think of them as an instrument panel. They tell you when a new model is better on your work and when it is merely different. They tell you whether a prompt revision helped one slice and quietly hurt another. They tell you whether a new tool description raised completion rate but also raised latency or cost. They tell you whether your agent can still handle the failures that hurt you last month. Without that loop, a team runs a series of hopeful anecdotes, not a production system.
Reliability did not get easier

It is tempting to believe that more capable models dissolved the old reliability problem. They did not. Samuel Colvin says, "We still want to build reliable scalable applications and that is still hard. Arguably it's actually harder with Gen AI than it was before." Generative systems fail in a broader range of ways, including ways that look correct. Prompt design, retrieval, tool calling, context assembly, and business logic all interact.

That complexity makes a single score attractive, because one number would shrink the uncertainty to a familiar size. I think the right answer to complexity is a richer control system. The chapter describes it as representative tasks, credible scoring, production observability, regression sets from real failures, comparison loops, and a habit of turning mistakes into reusable tests.
The habit that matters

The chapter ends on the point I most want engineers to repeat. Once AI systems do work instead of suggesting it, measurement stops being optional. You cannot supervise every action, and you cannot reason from benchmark scores to production trust. Evals are not there to tell you whether your model is impressive. They tell you whether your system is safe to trust.

The question "Do we have evals?" is too small. A team can answer yes with one spreadsheet and one overworked engineer. The better question is whether you have an operating habit that turns a real failure into a better system.

So here is a concrete step. Take the last failure your AI system caused, even a small one that review let through. Write it down as a test case with a clear pass condition, and store it somewhere your team will run it again. That single case is the start of a control loop.

title: Build an eval habit from your own failures
excerpt: Five steps from Chapter 4 that a team can take this week to turn real failures into evals, traces, and a habit that keeps improving the system.

source.title: Chapter 4 — Evals Are the Control System
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 4 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 4 of my book argues that evals are a control system for delegated work. A control system sounds heavy. It does not have to start that way. Here are five steps from the chapter's checklist that a team can take this week.
Start from real work

First, mine your evals from real failures. Naman Jain gives the rule: "Your task should be natural and sourced from the real world and then you should be able to reliably grade them." His team crawls the commit history of real repositories and finds commits related to performance optimization. You can copy the recipe. Pick a fix that mattered in your own history. Revert it. Hand the agent the broken state. Score whether it gets back to the known-good commit. I find this beats a benchmark built in a conference room, because the task is real and the grade is stable.

Early on, seed the set by hand. Samuel Colvin describes the common practice: people have "some subset of data that's been like human annotated." Humans know which failures are expensive. If a class of mistake bit your team three times last month, it belongs in the test set from now on.

Second, grade how the system got there, not only where it landed. Two runs can end on the same diff. One took a safe route. The other deleted a failing test to turn red into green. A check on the final files alone passes both. Score whether the agent reached the known-good end state, and inspect the path.
Weight and trace

Third, weight your slices by consequence, not frequency. Application evals mix objective checks with human review and carry slice-level metrics instead of one score. The slices are not equally important. A single averaged score hides the failures that cost the most. Let a rare but expensive failure outweigh a common trivial one. Ask whether the output was correct, and also whether it was usable, safe, timely, and cheap enough for this workflow.

Fourth, instrument every production run as a trace before you think you need it. A trace you never captured is a regression case you can never recover. Dat Ngo of Arize says, "code doesn't audit agents or harnesses — it's actually the telemetry that does that." Phil Hetzel says observability and evals are "actually the same problem from a systems perspective." Production traces feed the next offline eval set. A failed coding task can become a benchmark slice. A costly retrieval miss can become a dataset item.
Ask the habit question

Fifth, replace the inventory question with the habit question. "Do we have evals?" is too small. Ask whether you have a habit that turns this month's real failure into next month's regression test. Someone has to own the datasets. Someone has to decide how failures are labeled. Someone has to adjudicate when an automatic judge disagrees with expert review. In immature teams, one careful engineer and one spreadsheet carry all of this. That is a fair beginning but not a durable end state.

A short plan for the week might look like this. On Monday, pick one painful failure from your history and write it as a case. On Tuesday, decide how you will grade the path as well as the result. Midweek, name the one slice that costs you most when it fails. On Thursday, confirm that production runs leave traces you can replay. On Friday, name an owner for the dataset.
You will not finish a mature eval program in a week. You will have a seed, an owner, and a loop. The chapter's point is that the loop matters more than the size of the first set.

title: The patch that looked fine and stalled the backfills
excerpt: A rate-limiting patch compiles, passes tests, and still drifts production. A scene from Chapter 4 shows what a regression case is for.

source.title: Chapter 4 — Evals Are the Control System
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 4 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: The easiest way to see what evals are for is to watch what happens without them. Chapter 4 gives me a scene for that. It follows Meridian, the fictional payments team from the previous chapter, after they move from small safe edits to multi-file implementation tasks.
A tidy pull request

The agent receives a task. Add rate limiting to an internal API endpoint, thread the new behavior through a background job, and preserve an existing admin override. On first inspection the run looks good. The patch compiles. The tests pass. The pull request description is tidy. A reviewer glances at the diff and says what the chapter calls the most expensive sentence in modern engineering: looks fine.

Two days later support reports something odd. A class of admin-triggered backfills is stalling in production. Nothing is fully broken. Jobs queue longer than usual. Customers are not yet furious and engineers are not yet panicking. The system is drifting into a worse state.
What the postmortem found

The agent did implement rate limiting. It even mirrored the main service pattern correctly. But it also applied the same throttle to the backfill path, where the intended rule was different. That exception existed only in an old review comment and in the head of Meridian's most senior payments engineer. The code still type-checked. The unit tests still passed, because none covered the override path under production-like volume. The patch was locally plausible and globally wrong.

I like this scene because it is ordinary. These are not spectacular hallucinations. They are near-misses that survive review because each move looks reasonable. The model did not go insane. The system had no reliable way to notice that an important slice of behavior had regressed.

The scene also answers a common hope. Colvin says a coding agent can use type checking "to basically mark its own homework." That helps. Static checks, tests, and schemas catch the errors a machine can already define. But this patch cleared every one of those gates. Self-verification cannot certify that the whole change was correct. Production reliability needs several layers of evidence.
From lesson to instrument

Once Meridian sees the pattern, the eval work almost writes itself. They add a regression case for the admin override path. The team afterward calls it the admin-override regression. They mine earlier incidents for similar special-path behavior. They create a task slice for patches that touch both product logic and operations logic. They stop asking only whether a patch passes. They ask which real failure families it still protects against.

The chapter calls this a control system in practice. It converts an expensive lesson into a reusable instrument. Notice what moved. The knowledge lived in an old comment and in one senior engineer's memory. Now it lives in a test that runs every time, whoever is on call and whichever model wrote the patch.

Here is the takeaway I would carry. After your next incident, do not stop at the fix. Ask who held the knowledge that would have prevented it. Then write that knowledge as a case that fails when the behavior regresses. If the answer is one person's memory, you have found your next eval.

title: Context is the working set, not the knowledge base
excerpt: The book argues that AI systems fail when they assemble the wrong working set, not only when the model is weak. Here is the idea in short.

source.title: Chapter 5 — Context Is Infrastructure
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 5 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Useful AI systems do not fail only because the model is weak. Chapter 5 of my book makes a plain claim. They fail because the system cannot assemble the right working set of information at the right moment, in the right shape, at a cost the product can bear.

That claim moves context out of the prompt box. For a while, context looked like an input-field problem. You had a token limit and a collection of tricks for filling it. The chapter argues that this framing gets the problem backwards. Context is the substrate that decides what the system can notice at all.
Access is not context

Teams often treat access to more information as the same thing as better context. It is not. A company may hold millions of documents. A codebase may hold thousands of files. None of that guarantees the model sees the right few things for this task, in this turn.
So the unit I care about is the active working set. The question is what the model should look at right now to do this job well. It is a stricter question than what the model can reach in principle.
Kuba Rogut relays Jeff Dean on the sizing rule: you do not need a trillion tokens at once, you need the right million. The number worth instrumenting is how little of the index the answer needed.

Nupur Sharma's work at Qodo gives one mechanism. Models privilege the start and end of the window and degrade in the middle. A longer prompt does not buy more attention. It buys a wider blind spot. Her cue is concrete: when accuracy drops as you add retrieved documents, you are watching the middle get dropped. The fix is better assembly, such as summarization, graphs, and iterative retrieval. A bigger window does not fix it.
Misassembly is not hallucination

Teams often call the failure hallucination. Sometimes it is. Just as often it is context misassembly. The distinction matters because the remedy changes. Hallucination invites better model behavior. Misassembly invites better infrastructure.

There is a second reason to take this seriously. A stronger model raises both the return on good context and the cost of bad context. It does more with the right evidence in front of it. It also produces more persuasive nonsense when the context is badly assembled. A better model is a reason to invest more in context, not less.

For that reason, Chapter 5 puts context in the same bucket as harnesses, evals, runtimes, and security. These are engineered surroundings. They decide whether intelligence becomes useful. A machine colleague does not need infinite information. It needs the right binder.

Here is the takeaway for your own system. The next time your assistant disappoints, do not reach for a new model first. Look at what it was shown. Log what the system retrieved and how little of it the answer used. If accuracy falls as you add documents, change how you assemble the set before you change anything else.

title: A week of context checks for your retrieval system
excerpt: Five checks from the Chapter 5 checklist that a team can run in one week to find out whether context assembly or the model is the problem.

source.title: Chapter 5 — Context Is Infrastructure
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 5 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 5 of my book ends with a practical checklist. Five items. Each one is small enough to try in a day. Together they tell you whether your context system helps the work or only looks good in a diagram.
I will take them in the order a team could run them across a week.
Monday and Tuesday: look and measure

Start with one signal. Plot accuracy against the number of retrieved documents. If accuracy drops as you add documents, the middle of the context window is getting lost. The model is not getting dumber. The book's fix is better assembly, such as summarization, graphs, or iterative retrieval, not a bigger window.

Next, change what you instrument. Most teams track how big the index is. I suggest tracking how little of it the answer needed. Kuba Rogut relays Jeff Dean: you do not need a trillion tokens at once, you need the right million. So record how much of what you retrieved a task actually used. That number tells you where you are wasting attention and money.

On cost, Rajkumar Sakthivel's team at Tesco says 90 percent of AI cost is input: files, search results, and context you send in. Only 10 percent is output. His team cut input tokens by 94 percent on a public benchmark by retrieving relevant slices of a codebase instead of pasting whole files. He is careful to say that is a best case, and real setups will not match it. Treat it as a reason to measure, not as a target.
Wednesday and Thursday: match and separate

Now look at your retrieval mechanism. Match it to the shape of the answer. Use vector search when the answer is a single similar passage. Use graph traversal when the answer is a path along explicit relationships. Use keyword or metadata filters when exactness is what matters. Do not make one mechanism carry all three jobs. Mature systems layer them.

Then split your eval in two. Score retrieval and generation as separate questions. First, check whether the governing passage reached the assembled working set at all. That is a recall measure on the context layer. Only then score whether the model used it correctly. If you score only the final answer, a context-assembly bug looks exactly like a model getting dumber. You may then spend a model upgrade on a retrieval problem.
Friday: change a default

The last item is about people. When a fix depends on users opting in, assume almost no one will. GitHub learned this with its remote MCP server. After community contributions pushed it past a hundred tools, the agents got measurably worse. The first fixes were opt-in tool sets and dynamic discovery. Almost no one used them, because most users never touch the JSON config. GitHub changed the default instead and cut the initial tool-load context by 49 percent. The number of tools the agent could call did not fall. The number it had to read did.
So on Friday, find one place where your system relies on a setting nobody changes. Change the default.

By the end of the week you will have four facts: how accuracy moves with document count, how much context a task really uses, whether the right passage arrives, and which defaults carry your product. Write them on one page. That page is your first honest view of your context system, and it will tell you what to fix first.

title: The deduction that cited the wrong source
excerpt: A tax assistant at Hargrove ranked a public explainer above a senior attorney's matter note. The fix taught the team what context topology means.

source.title: Chapter 5 — Context Is Infrastructure
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 5 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 5 of my book follows a firm called Hargrove. Hargrove runs a tax practice. Its assistant began as a helpful chat surface. It summarizes documents, answers questions, and cites plausible authorities. Users like it. In the book I call this kind of system the High-Stakes Colleague: an assistant that works where evidence and provenance change the quality of the work.
After the novelty phase, users ask for something harder. They stop saying help me think. They say help me do the work.
The request

A tax associate asks the assistant to trace the support for a deduction a client has claimed for years. The assistant answers fluently. It cites a clean-looking authority, a public explainer whose wording matches the query almost perfectly. The answer reads as decisive.

It is also wrong for this client. The governing position lives in a matter note that a senior attorney wrote earlier, in a different file, under a jurisdiction the explainer never mentions. The system ranked the explainer first because nothing told it that a public article and a matter-specific note are different kinds of evidence.

I want to stay with this failure, because it is easy to misread. The model did not lack knowledge. It did not invent a source. The explainer was real. The system simply treated all text as interchangeable and ranked by closeness to the query. In the book I note that simplistic retrieval systems flatten everything into one searchable pile and act as if the only problem were semantic similarity.
The remedy

The remedy was not a smarter model. The team typed its knowledge topology into the system. In practice that meant three changes. Source typing ranks internal precedent above public background. Access boundaries apply per matter. The retrieval surface carries provenance, so the associate can see which layer an answer came from.

Context topology is my name for this idea. Different kinds of information should not be treated as interchangeable text. A draft contract is not signed language. An old Slack discussion is not a policy. A matter note from a senior attorney is not a general explainer from a public source. What matters is what kind of thing a document is, how trustworthy it is, how recent it is, and whether the task needs literal quotation or background.

Chau Tran's Glean work makes the same point operational. Much of it is filtering on signals the corpus already carries: the user's permission scope, the freshness of the source, and the document's role in the organization. That filtering runs before the reranker, so material the task should never see never reaches the window. Without it, ranking on raw embedding similarity will happily surface a deprecated wiki page that reads almost exactly like the current one.

The chapter says that in high-stakes work, a system that is 90 percent right for unclear reasons can still be professionally unusable. The associate needs to know why an answer is right. Provenance gives that.

Here is the lesson to carry away. List the kinds of documents your assistant can retrieve. For each pair, ask whether one should outrank the other. If the answer is yes, write that rule into the system, and show the source type next to every citation. At Hargrove, the misranked matter note became the scar the rest of the build-out was designed around. You can learn the same lesson from a list, before a client pays for it.

title: Agents are stateful workflows with probabilistic nodes
excerpt: Chapter 6 argues that a production agent needs durable state, recovery, and human review points. A chat transcript cannot supply them.

source.title: Chapter 6 — Runtimes, State, and the Human Control Plane
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 6 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A chatbot can get away with amnesia. A production agent cannot. That is the opening line of Chapter 6 of my book, and the rest of the chapter works out what follows from it.

A chat system can answer a question, emit a patch, or suggest a draft, and then disappear. Once you ask a system to do work that unfolds across time, tools, failures, and approvals, the center of gravity moves. The question is no longer whether the model can produce a smart next token. The question is whether the surrounding system can preserve intent, survive interruption, recover from error, expose its progress, and stop in the right places for human review.
A transcript is not state

Many impressive demos break here. The model may be good enough. The context may be strong. But the builders made the system like a conversation when it needed to be a workflow. It loses track of what already happened. A retry repeats work or performs the same action twice. An approval arrives after the risky step. In my words, the agent does not fail because it is unintelligent. It fails because it has nowhere durable to stand.

A transcript cannot be that place. It does not cleanly show task progress, pending approvals, completed tool calls, or which intermediate outputs are binding. Samuel Colvin puts the break point simply: "Once we get into longer running workflows, that's where it really becomes a problem." A short answer can be regenerated. A half-finished legal workflow cannot.

Preeti Somal gives the best backbone for the chapter. She says that at the core of agentic AI applications is a complicated workflow that needs to handle state potentially over long periods of time, with human interaction for approvals. From that I draw one sentence: useful agentic systems are stateful workflows with probabilistic decision nodes.

This ends a false choice. People sometimes say workflows are rigid and agents are flexible, so choosing workflows means giving up agency. The chapter argues the opposite. Workflow structure is what makes useful agency survivable. It explains why pause and resume matter, why retries should not live in ad hoc prompt logic, and why approvals belong inside execution.
The human control plane

The chapter's title concept follows. The human control plane is the set of interfaces, approvals, visibility layers, and intervention mechanisms through which people supervise delegated machine work. I treat it as an architectural layer. It is not a crutch on the way to full autonomy.

A chat transcript is usually not enough for supervision. Operators need queue views, roll-up summaries, pending-review surfaces, and clean intervention points. If the only way to supervise an agent is to read back through thousands of tokens, the control plane does not exist yet. Eric Zakariasson states the need in plain English: "Here's what everyone is working on... and here's what you as a human need to review."
None of this means a person approves every step. Control is a gradient. The design task is to place the few checkpoints that carry the most judgment.

Here is the takeaway. Pick one agent workflow you run today. Write down what it must remember if it stops halfway: the plan, the finished tool calls, the pending questions for a human. If that list lives only in the prompt window, you have a chat, not a runtime. Move the list into stored state first, then decide where a person should step in.

title: Runtime decisions to settle before you add more agents
excerpt: Five checklist items from Chapter 6 turned into steps a team can take this week, from replay versus snapshots to isolated environments for each worker.

source.title: Chapter 6 — Runtimes, State, and the Human Control Plane
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 6 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 6 of my book closes with five checklist items about agent runtimes. The chapter states them as principles. Here I turn them into steps a team can take this week. Do them in this order, because each one shapes the next.
Decide how the system continues

First, choose replay or snapshots on purpose. A replay design keeps an event history and rebuilds state from what happened. Reach for it when causality and auditability are the point, so state emerges from recorded steps and not from opaque frozen blobs. A snapshot design saves checkpoints of working state. Reach for it when fast continuation and elaborate live state dominate, so pause and resume stay cheap.

This week, hold a short meeting and write one sentence: our system needs replay, or snapshots, because of this. If you cannot finish the sentence, you are not ready to build either. The chapter says teams at this point are making the decisions mature distributed systems always make: what gets persisted, what gets recomputed, and what must be auditable.

Second, place checkpoints where judgment lives. The design question is not how to keep a human in every loop. It is where the few checkpoints that carry the most judgment should sit, before, during, or after execution. In a coding factory, subagents might explore, draft, and run validations alone, while merge decisions, large architectural changes, and dependency additions wait for review. Mark those on your workflow diagram and remove approvals everywhere else.
Decide how the system spends and isolates

Third, route to the cheapest model that still passes the eval, and no cheaper. Which model runs a step is a control-plane decision made per task. It is not a global default chosen once. Laurie Voss at Arize says to use cheap models for simple queries and expensive models in your agent for complex ones. But routing adds a failure surface. A misroute hands a hard task to a cheap model that quietly botches it. So run your eval on the cheaper route first, and keep verification in place behind it.

Fourth, give every parallel worker its own isolated, ephemeral environment. If several agents share one dev setup, they collide on the same branch, ports, and database. One agent's migration can break the others mid-run. A git worktree is enough for trusted edits. Untrusted, side-effecting work needs a VM. Rene Brandel at Casco warns that if you just use containers, that is not an isolation layer, because agent code can get root and move laterally. Audit how your workers are isolated today and mark which ones run untrusted work.
Decide who sees what

Fifth, design observability for two audiences at once. Engineers need deep inspection of one trajectory. Operators need roll-up supervision across many. Good traces capture plans, tool calls, state changes, intermediate outputs, timings, and the boundaries between durable steps. Add redaction and risk-based views from the start. Richer traces buy trust and retention risk in the same breath.

At the end of the week you should hold five short decisions on one page. Replay or snapshots. Where humans review. Which model runs which step. How each worker is isolated. Who sees which trace. Add no new agent until that page exists. More workers multiply whatever your runtime already lacks.

title: When Meridian's subagents disagreed
excerpt: Meridian asked its agents to investigate, patch, and report, and parallel work turned into fragments. The scene shows why coordination is the missing piece.

source.title: Chapter 6 — Runtimes, State, and the Human Control Plane
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 6 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: In my book, a team called Meridian runs what I call a Software Factory. That means a repo and a quality system prepared so that agents can do real engineering work. By Chapter 6, Meridian has rebuilt its repo and added eval slices that catch special-path mistakes. Small delegated work goes well.

Then the team raises its ambition. Instead of isolated patches, it asks the system to investigate a bug, spawn a few subagents, inspect a cluster of files, propose a fix, run checks, and prepare a reviewable summary for a human.
What went wrong

A second class of problems appears. One subagent finds the relevant failure. Another, working off a slightly older branch of understanding, proposes a different patch. A retry of the validation step reruns something the first attempt had already completed. The human reviewer receives fragments of work, not a coherent roll-up.

I describe the result as a workshop full of talented workers without a foreman's board, without station history, and without a clean shift handoff. The system still has intelligence and context. It has no stable execution semantics.

Notice what did not fail. The model was fine. The workers were competent. The failure came from the space between them. More workers mean more intermediate artifacts, more duplicated effort, and more state to coordinate. In the chapter I say that parallelism without recomposition is just chaos at higher speed. The design challenge is not how to spawn more workers. It is how to merge, compare, inspect, and route their outputs so the human stays oriented.
What the book offers

The book gives a few pieces of the answer. Independence must be enforced by the environment, not merely declared in the task split. Each worker needs its own isolated, ephemeral environment, or one agent's migration breaks the others mid-run.

Lou Bichard at Ona sharpens the diagnosis. He argues the runtime is solved, with "many options for this now, sandboxes and containers", and so are triggers and orchestration. "The thing that's missing," he says, "is coordination." He means an agent-native primitive that lets parallel workers pick up tasks, signal completion, and hand off without a human stitching them together. His candidate building blocks are "state machines, by building out workflows."

The chapter also notes that teams shipping production multi-agent systems have not agreed on an answer. Each substitutes a known mechanism for the missing one. Factory runs features serially with one active writer. Anthropic's long-running agents write a contract to files on disk before any code is produced. Others use state machines with durable execution. Three substitutes for one primitive that does not yet exist.

The lesson for a team like Meridian is concrete. Before you add a fourth subagent, decide how you will answer three questions. Which worker owns each task? Where is the shared record of what is done, so a retry does not repeat finished work? Where does the human see one roll-up instead of fragments? If you cannot answer, run work serially with one writer until you can. That is slower. It also removes the coordination problem by construction.

title: Build so that an agent being wrong is survivable
excerpt: A model should never enforce its own power. Chapter 7 argues for sandboxes, narrow scopes, and boundaries that hold when the model is wrong.

source.title: Chapter 7 — Security, Identity, and High-Stakes Trust
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 7 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: A helpful model can get away with being vague about power. An acting system cannot. That pair of sentences opens Chapter 7, and they hold the whole chapter in small form.

Once an agent can read across accounts, call tools, execute code, or keep working after you have looked away, trust stops being a judgment about how smart the model sounds. It becomes an architecture question. Who is this system acting as? What can it reach? What can it do without asking again? What evidence remains afterward? How fast can we reduce or revoke its power?
The model is not the enforcement layer
The chapter gives one rule I would like you to repeat. A model can never be the final enforcement layer for its own power.

If an agent can execute code, browse untrusted content, open files, or chain across tools, the design must assume someone can induce it into bad behavior. A malicious instruction can do it. So can a poisoned page, a badly described tool, or a plain misunderstanding. The cause matters less than the consequence.

So the principle is blunt. Assume the agent will sometimes be wrong, and build so that being wrong is survivable. In classic software, developers wrote the code paths and could know them ahead of time. In agentic software, the system chooses among many paths at runtime. The model may improvise. The environment should fail closed.
Where the boundaries live

This pushes security talk toward runtime design. It becomes a talk about operating system boundaries, execution isolation, token scope, credential lifetimes, and mediation layers. These decide what the system can do when the model is confused, manipulated, or simply too eager.

The chapter cites Fouad Matin's security guidance for coding agents at OpenAI. It names four controls as the default-on baseline: sandboxing, network restriction, privilege boundaries, and human review. Each one bounds a different failure. A bad command, exfiltration, over-reach when the agent is wrong, and the trajectory the first three let through.

I am not arguing against alignment work. There is a serious discipline devoted to what a model is disposed to do, refuse, and value. The book covers a different layer. It covers the engineering around the model: the boundaries, identities, sandboxes, and audit trails that must hold even when the model's inner alignment is imperfect.

Narrow powers help in a second way. They reduce the number of tempting but unsafe paths the model can wander into. A tighter design often makes the system easier to reason about, not only safer. The chapter puts it this way: safe delegation comes from making carelessness less powerful, not from asking the model to be careful.
None of this is a promise that nothing will go wrong. Controls bound failures. They do not remove the need to expect them.
One thing to do

Pick one agent you run today. Find the step where it holds the most power. Write down the worst plausible mistake it could make there, whether from a bad instruction or a plain error. Then ask one question: would that mistake be survivable? If the answer is no, narrow the power at that step before you spend another hour improving the prompt.

title: Five agent security steps a team can take this week
excerpt: Chapter 7 ends with a short checklist. Here is how a team can turn it into five concrete actions before the next sprint ends.

source.title: Chapter 7 — Security, Identity, and High-Stakes Trust
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 7 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: The practical checklist at the end of Chapter 7 has five items. Each one fits in a week of work for a small team. None of them needs a new product. They need a few honest conversations and some editing of configuration.
Start with the agents you already run

First, check whether your agents run the four-controls baseline by default. The chapter names them: sandboxing, network restriction, privilege boundaries, and human review. Each stops a different failure. Sit with one agent and ask which of the four it has. Treat any gap as a defect now, not as hardening for after an incident.

Second, run a survivability test at each step. The chapter asks you to build for the idea that the agent will sometimes be wrong. So for each step, ask whether a mistake there is survivable before you ask whether the agent could make it. Write the answer next to the step. Where the answer is no, add a gate or narrow the power.

Third, write one default-permission row per agent. Do not write one blanket policy. The chapter gives examples. A research agent may need no write access at all. A support agent may read account metadata but not issue refunds. A legal workflow may need broad retrieval but no authority to send anything externally. Think about the stage of the workflow too, not only the agent as a whole. A scope that looks harmless alone can compound once it pairs with retrieval, persistence, and retries.
Then look at connections and credentials

Fourth, apply the governance test before you add a tool server. The chapter says that if a new connection grows your agents' reach faster than your team can answer who can call this, with what scope, and where it is logged, then standardization has expanded your attack surface. Make that a gate. No new server joins until someone writes down the three answers.

The chapter quotes Tun Shwe at Lenses: "Your insecure MCP server won't survive production." The failures he points to are mundane. Authentication treated as a configuration option. Tool descriptions trusted as input. Servers exposed publicly because internal routing was harder.

Fifth, hunt for standing credentials. Search your agent configuration for long-lived API keys and for personal access tokens borrowed from an operator. The chapter calls a standing credential a red flag. An agent on a borrowed key is not delegated authority. It is impersonation with no expiry and nothing to revoke. The shape the chapter points toward is a short-lived, scoped token bound to a session, a user, and a task.
A realistic plan for the week

On day one, list your agents. On day two, mark which of the four controls each has. On day three, write the permission rows. On day four, review every connected tool server against the governance test. On day five, replace one standing credential with a scoped one, and log what you could not fix yet.

You will not finish everything. That is fine. The chapter does not promise that a checklist makes a system safe. It asks you to make carelessness less powerful, one agent at a time, and to leave a written record of what you changed and what remains open.

The takeaway is small and specific. By Friday, you should hold a single page: one permission row per agent, one answer to the three governance questions per tool server, and a short list of credentials still to replace.

title: The day a client disputes what the assistant filed
excerpt: A scene from Chapter 7 shows why audit trails matter as much as blocking bad actions, and what a partner can say when asked what happened.

source.title: Chapter 7 — Security, Identity, and High-Stakes Trust
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 7 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 7 contains a short scene I want to retell. It teaches one lesson about trust, and it is easy to miss because it is not about prevention.

The scene runs in Hargrove, the running example I use through the book. Hargrove's assistant helped file a position. Later, a client disputes it. A partner has to answer one question: what did the system actually do?
Two possible answers

In the first version, the assistant reached its documents through a mediation layer. The answer exists. The trajectory shows which matter files the assistant retrieved, which validation engine it called, and which draft it surfaced for review. It also shows the authority behind each step. The assistant worked under a read-only token scoped to this matter. It had no authority to send anything to the client.
In the second version, nothing was recorded. The chapter is direct about this case. Without a trail, the honest answer would be a shrug.

That contrast carries the lesson. Security talk often focuses on blocking bad actions. The chapter says blocking is only half the requirement. In high-stakes environments, trust also depends on reconstructing what happened. Which sources were consulted? Which tool calls were made? Which permissions were exercised? Which output reached review, and by what path? If a regulator asks questions later, the organization needs more than a statement that the model was generally aligned. It needs evidence.
What the trail does

I call this inspectability, and I treat it as part of the security argument, not a side topic. Rich traces, approval logs, trajectory views, and reviewable histories let an institution turn bounded autonomy into something it can defend. The chapter draws on Joel Hron's high-stakes framing. The answer there is not unrestricted autonomy under perfect prevention. It is constrained execution plus inspectable paths. The system does meaningful work and leaves behind a trail that domain experts can examine.

Notice how the scene depends on earlier design choices. The read-only, matter-scoped token is least privilege. The mediation layer is what made the trail possible in the first place. The partner can answer calmly because the architecture was built to be questioned. Inspection works as the last layer on top of the others.
The tension the chapter admits

I do not want to present this as simple. Detailed traces can expose sensitive data, internal reasoning artifacts, or privileged content. A trail that anyone can read becomes its own risk. So the chapter asks for selective retention, role-based visibility, redaction strategies, and different surfaces for operators, reviewers, and auditors. The tension is not an argument against inspection. It is an argument for governing inspection properly.
The takeaway

Ask yourself the partner's question about your own agent today. If a client or a regulator asked what it did last Tuesday, could you name the sources it consulted, the tools it called, and the permissions it used? If you could not, start with the cheapest fix. Pick one agent and record, for each run, the tool calls and the authority used. Then decide who may read that record, and write that down too.

title: Voice is a stress test for the whole agent system
excerpt: Text chat forgives weak design. Chapter 8 argues that voice removes that mercy and shows whether the loop around the model is sound.

source.title: Chapter 8 — Realtime, Voice, and the Cost of Being Interruptible
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 8 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Text chat flatters AI systems. It hides latency behind a blinking cursor. It tolerates awkward pauses. It lets a weak handoff look like thoughtful reflection. Users have time to scroll, reinterpret, and quietly repair what the system failed to make clear. A lot of fragile AI feels smarter in text simply because text is forgiving.
Chapter 8 starts from that observation and makes one argument. Voice removes the mercy, so voice shows whether the rest of your architecture was honest.
Voice strips away excuses
The field often treats voice as a charming frontier, a natural interface that needs slightly better models. I think that framing is too soft. Voice matters because it takes away the excuses.

If the context architecture is weak, the system fumbles the thread. If the runtime is brittle, interruptions break it. If the security model is sloppy, approvals become too casual and authority too ambient. If the control plane is underdesigned, the user has to rescue the interaction constantly. If the tool layer is slow, the product sounds incompetent no matter how good the model is alone.

The themes from earlier chapters are all still present: scaffolding, evals, context, runtime design, authority boundaries, and human control. Realtime compresses them into milliseconds. Problems that chat can hide become audible. Kwindla Hultman Kramer draws the line by the clock, and the chapter quotes him: real time is anything inside "conversational latency of a few hundred milliseconds or less."
Where the test actually lives

You might expect the hard part to be speech recognition or speech synthesis. The chapter says the real test is narrower and harder. It is timing, overlap, and interruption, the three ways a live conversation breaks. Even as speech models improve, systems still wait too long, cut in too aggressively, or lose coherence when the human changes direction mid-stream.

A model can be perfectly articulate and still fail all three. The thing under test is whether the system can coordinate listening, reasoning, tool use, and speaking under live pressure. That is a property of the loop around the model, not of the model by itself.

This is why I describe a realtime system as the most unforgiving version of a general truth. Trustworthy AI depends on the loop around the model. Voice makes that loop visible because the human is still there to feel every systems defect as behavior. They hear the hesitation. They hear the stale answer.
What to do with this

The practical reading is a change in where you look. When a voice agent feels bad, do not reach first for a better voice or a larger model. Ask which layer failed. Was it context, runtime, authority, control, or a slow tool? The chapter's view is that teams who think they are building a speech product often discover they are building an orchestration product.

The chapter closes with three short lines that I would happily see on a wall. Dependable AI is not merely a property of good answers. It is a property of good loops. And realtime interaction is where that truth becomes impossible to ignore.

So the takeaway is a habit. The next time your agent disappoints you in a voice test, write down the failure in terms of the loop, not the model. Name the layer. Fix that layer. You will also find that the same fix improves your text chat, where nobody was complaining yet.

title: Five voice agent changes a team can try this week
excerpt: Chapter 8 ends with five practical rules for realtime agents. Here is how to apply each one in a week without rebuilding your stack.

source.title: Chapter 8 — Realtime, Voice, and the Cost of Being Interruptible
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 8 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 8 ends with a practical checklist for realtime and voice agents. Five rules. Here is how I would turn each into work for this week.
Fix the latency budget first

The first rule is to spend your latency budget on first audio, not on silence. A quick spoken acknowledgment followed by a slower answer beats a long silent pause followed by a polished one. The chapter notes that streaming partial understanding can rescue a system whose deeper reasoning takes longer.

Start by measuring the whole loop, not one stage. Neil Zeghidour at Gradium AI sets the target for natural conversation at "around 200 milliseconds" for the entire stack of understanding, producing an answer, and pronouncing it. Kwindla Hultman Kramer says to watch the tail. In his words, "you care a lot if your P95 goes up above 800, 900, 1,000 milliseconds for the entire voice-to-voice response chain." Record your own P95 from voice to voice. Then add a spoken acknowledgment before any slow step, and measure again.

The chapter also warns that tool calls become the bottleneck as speech layers improve. Zeghidour says a tool call "between 500 milliseconds and 4 seconds" gives you a dead line at the long end. So list your slowest tools and time them.
Match the interaction to the system you have

The second rule concerns half-duplex systems. Most production speech-to-speech systems cannot listen and speak at once. Structured, turn-based flows survive that limit. Open-ended companion chat does not, because the model reads every interjection as a barge-in. This week, decide which kind of flow your agent serves. If it is open-ended, narrow it to a structured flow. Do not patch the limit with longer silence thresholds.

The third rule inverts confirmation cost on purpose. Voice manufactures false confidence, so the warmer the interface, the cheaper approval feels. Go through your agent's actions and rank them by consequence. For the top few, make confirmation more deliberate: repeat the key detail back, and ask for a clear yes. Leave low-stakes actions light.
Reuse the agent you already trust

The fourth rule says to wrap voice around your strongest existing agent and not rebuild one. Luke Harries at ElevenLabs puts it plainly in the chapter: "I've already got my agent. I spent loads of time doing the evals." Keep the tools, the evals, and the workflow logic. If the underlying system is weak, voice will expose that faster. So run your existing evals against the agent before you add the voice layer, and fix what fails.

The fifth rule asks you to give the system a way to say "I'm not sure" out loud. In voice the human watches it hesitate in real time. Write three spoken phrases for uncertainty: one to clarify, one to confirm, and one to hand off. Then check that an escalation path exists behind the third.
A plan for the week

Monday, measure P95 and list slow tools. Tuesday, add acknowledgments. Wednesday, rank actions and tighten confirmations. Thursday, run existing evals on the core agent. Friday, write the uncertainty phrases and test the handoff.
The takeaway is one number and one habit. Know your voice-to-voice P95, and never leave the caller in silence while a slow step runs.

title: When a caller interrupts, your runtime gets tested
excerpt: A support-call scene from Chapter 8 shows that interruption handling is about execution semantics, not UX polish, and what to design for.

source.title: Chapter 8 — Realtime, Voice, and the Cost of Being Interruptible
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 8 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Chapter 8 opens its main scene with a support call. I want to walk through it, because it teaches one lesson: turn-taking is a runtime problem wearing a UX costume.

Picture Hargrove's assistant, the running example in the book, on a live call. The client's account is locked. Their case crosses billing and compliance rules. Their patience is running out in real time. The agent must understand messy speech, notice that the caller interrupted to add a crucial exception, retrieve the right policy, check the client record, decide whether to act or escalate, and explain what it is doing. It must also avoid sounding either lost or overconfident.
Three moments that break

The chapter picks out a few moments. In the first, the caller corrects their own account number halfway through a sentence. The system has to revise state. In the second, the caller says, "No, wait, that was the old policy." The system has to tell abandoned context from active context. In the third, the agent says "One moment while I check that" and then goes silent. The caller does not experience a neutral backend delay. They experience incompetence.

Then comes the case I find most instructive. The agent has already begun a retrieval step when the caller reveals that the account belongs to a different region. If the runtime cannot cancel, redirect, or downgrade the old plan cleanly, the system starts answering with stale assumptions. The human hears a conversational failure. The root problem is execution semantics.
Questions that belong to the runtime

It is tempting to file interruption handling under polish. The chapter says that is too shallow. When a human cuts the system off, what state is preserved? Which partial output is discarded? Does a tool call continue in the background, and if so, how is the result surfaced later? If the user answers a question indirectly, how much of the prior plan stays binding? If a user correction and a returning tool result arrive at once, which one wins?

None of these is a copywriting question. They are the same kind of question you ask of any durable workflow, now asked under a clock. The chapter adds that a spoken system must manage state in public. It needs a runtime that can pause, redirect, summarize, and resume without making the user rebuild everything by hand.

The security boundaries must also survive the change of medium. A friendly voice does not make overscoped authority less dangerous. The chapter goes further: because voice feels human, people approve more casually, so confirmation for consequential actions has to be more deliberate.
The takeaway

Take your own agent and write the support-call script for it. Include a mid-sentence correction, an abandoned policy, and a late discovery that changes the plan while a retrieval step is running. Then walk each case through your runtime on paper. For each one, write down what state is kept, what is discarded, and what the caller hears. Wherever you cannot answer, you have found a runtime gap. Fix it there, in the execution layer, before you touch the script the agent speaks.
